item.title: Hegseth's public execution plan meets the age of viral violence
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement that the Fort Hood shooter's execution will be livestreamed reflects a shift toward putting raw, real-world violence on display for unlimited audiences.

Why it matters: The Trump administration has made a show of flexing American power, sometimes with grisly footage. Now, it's preparing to make the government's ultimate punishment available for all to see.

The big picture: Americans are increasingly encountering shocking images on their phones, often without warning. Graphic footage of Charlie Kirk's assassination spread widely across social media, searing in the brains of social media users — often young ones.

  • Since Oct. 7, 2023, footage from the Hamas attacks and Israel's military campaign in Gaza has circulated online. Some videos have spread from Telegram to social platforms like X, where clips are easy to find.
  • Footage of the August 2025 killing of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte train went viral across X, stirring debate about crime and public safety. President Trump later said he had watched the video and wished he hadn't.

A livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution would be the first known public broadcast of a lawful execution, according to death penalty experts interviewed by Reuters.

  • Public executions are increasingly rare worldwide. In recent years, most have taken place in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.

Friction point: Tech companies are now facing the question of whether they would allow the Pentagon to livestream the execution on their platforms. Hasan, who killed 13 people in 2009 at the Fort Hood Army base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3.

  • TikTok and Kick said that livestreaming the event would violate their policies, The Verge reported.
  • YouTube, Meta, X and Twitch did not respond to The Verge's requests for comment.

Yes, but: Elon Musk has positioned X, in particular, as a bulwark against internet censorship in the name of free speech. Hegseth's plan is putting the limits of that free-speech philosophy to a new test.

  • The platform defended its decision to keep graphic content of the Kirk shooting on the platform, saying: "We will continue to stand against violence and censorship, ensuring this platform amplifies truth and open dialogue for everyone."
  • After a bishop was stabbed during a livestreamed church service in Australia in 2024, X defied government demands to remove footage of the attack worldwide.

Zoom out: Hegseth's announcement raises the prospect of reversing America's nearly century-long retreat from public executions.

  • He justified making the execution public, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
  • The 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky, which drew 20,000 spectators, is widely considered America's last public execution.
  • A modern-day livestreamed execution could reach billions.

The intrigue: Vice President JD Vance questioned Friday whether the execution would actually be livestreamed and said he wouldn't watch if it were.

  • Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) posted: "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. ... Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent."
  • Trump told reporters he had approved the decision to livestream the execution.

The bottom line: America spent nearly a century moving away from public executions. Now, with real-world violence just a click away, the U.S. government is preparing to show one to the world.

item.title: Trump rages over Nobel Peace Prize loss
item.description:
President Trump lashed out late Friday night after he once again did not win the Nobel Peace Prize he has openly coveted.

Why it matters: The award is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about frequently and believes he deserves.

  • This year's prize went instead to a former judge of a court Trump has sanctioned and called "rogue" and "evil."
  • Navi Pillay, the winner, reacted to the award by saying world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war," according to the AP.

What he's saying: "I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else! In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel. I don't know what the woman has done," Trump said in a Truth Social post of nearly 600 words that went up just before midnight on Friday.

  • "I settled 8 Wars, with letters being sent from every President and Prime Minister from the countries that I helped to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, and I'm about to settle, or win, two more, Iran and, Russia/Ukraine," Trump wrote.
  • "They're both happening at breakneck speed but, forget them, it's the 8 that I've already settled, any one of which, in particular, Pakistan and India, would be far more than necessary to win the Nobel Prize. In actuality, I should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1."

Between the lines: Pillay, this year's winner, is a former judge of the International Criminal Court and also the former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

  • Nobel officials said she received the honor "for her efforts to promote peace and international law."
  • Originally from South Africa, Pillay, 85, also served as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

Zoom in: Trump took aim at that UN association as well.

  • "In all of the Wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations—they were of no help. The United States of America, represented by me, as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't," he said.

The intrigue: Trump also blasted Norway, as he's previously done over Nobel snubs, though the country doesn't award the prize.

  • "This is an indelible stain on Norway, one that will never be forgotten. The Nobel 'Peace' Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!"

The bottom line: The president didn't hold back making his case for why he should have won — and why his loss was a personal snub.

item.title: U.S. official: Trump cut deal with Putin after Zelensky ignored his requests
item.description:
President Trump decided to make a diesel fuel deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored half a dozen U.S. requests to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, a U.S. official with direct knowledge told Axios.

Why it matters: Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin sparked a new crisis with Ukraine and threatens to derail a new push by the Trump administration for a deal to end the war.

  • "Zelensky is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the good will that he has built with Trump over the last six months," the U.S. official said.
  • Zelensky, in an interview with Axios after the announcement, said he was blindsided by the deal, which he called "not fair and not honest" and an unwarranted gift to Putin.

Driving the news: Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries in recent months were highly effective and caused an energy crisis in Russia.

  • Russia imposed a ban on diesel exports in response, which added more pressure to global diesel markets under strain from the war in Iran.
  • Zelensky told Trump and his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that he was prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if the Russians halted attacks on Ukrainian power plants.
  • The U.S. official said Trump wanted Ukraine to unilaterally stop attacking Russian refineries because the strikes were contributing to high gas prices in America.
  • Trump didn't see the attacks on refineries as equivalent to Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid, the U.S. official said.

Inside the room: During eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner told a Ukrainian negotiating team that the president was expected to speak to Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

  • They were told that Trump decided to move forward after Ukraine ignored multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, which were directly affecting U.S. consumers.
  • A Ukrainian official claimed that during the talks, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could cut off Ukraine from U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests.
  • The U.S. official denied such a threat was made and said Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, Witkoff and Kushner said.
  • "The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the U.S., too," the U.S. official said.

Zoom in: The official said the new crisis over the diesel deal erupted after the U.S. mediators had constructive talks with Ukrainian and European diplomats in Miami on Friday.

  • The main focus was on finalizing security guarantees that the U.S., Europe and NATO would provide to Ukraine as part of a deal to end the war.
  • New proposals for territorial solutions were also raised.
  • Witkoff and Kushner presented a postwar package for Ukraine that included ways to fund reconstruction and rebuild the Ukrainian military, as well as ideas on how to deal with budget deficits stemming from the war.
  • The participants also discussed a roadmap for Ukraine's accession to the EU and the relationship Ukraine would have with NATO after the war ends.
  • In addition, Witkoff and Kushner raised the possibility of a Europe-Russia postwar security framework that could appeal to both sides.

What to watch: Witkoff and Kushner briefed the Ukrainians and Europeans on potential energy deals with Russia that the U.S. hopes would bring down energy prices and induce Russia to make concessions in peace talks, the U.S. official said.

What's next: The U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner are considering visiting Moscow and Kyiv next week to discuss peace proposals, but it's unclear how Friday's blowup will affect their plans.

  • "Putin is hitting [Ukraine] hard but we think he is open to a discussion on ending the war. We want to work on a new proposal that will be good enough for him in order to get him to stop," the U.S. official said.

Yes, but: During his 90-minute phone call with Trump, Putin declined to commit to resuming peace talks with Ukraine, his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters.

  • He said that Ukrainian strikes on Moscow and other cities during the Russian parliamentary elections "thwarted the possibility of an immediate resumption of the negotiation process."
  • "The president said, we will think about when these negotiations can be resumed," Ushakov added.

item.title: JD Vance says he won't watch livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance said Friday he won't watch a potential livestream of the convicted Fort Hood shooter's execution, which President Trump told reporters he had approved.

Why it matters: Vance questioned whether the execution would actually be public but joined a small chorus of Republicans opposed to watching the execution, which is set to be conducted by a firing squad in December.

What they're saying: "Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters on Friday.

  • "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's all through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it."

Yes, but: Trump's comments came during a separate press gaggle on Friday, where he was asked if he had authorized or approved the livestream of the execution.

  • "Did I approve? Absolutely, I approve."

Driving the news: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in an interview Thursday that Americans would be able to watch the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting.

  • "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it. ... People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," he said.
  • AP later reported that the execution would be livestreamed.
  • If it goes forward, Hasan's execution will be the first public one in 90 years, and the first military execution since 1961.

Zoom in: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) condemned plans to make the execution public in a Thursday night X post.

  • "Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America," the outgoing senator said.
  • Utah Sen. John Curtis (R) said in an X post, "Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent."
  • "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity."

The other side: Some GOP politicians, like Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.), welcomed the livestream.

  • "Excellent. Public execution is what this terrorist deserves. We will be watching," he said in a post on X.

Editor's note: This story was updated with comments from President Trump.

item.title: Exclusive: Zelensky tells Axios Trump's diesel deal with Putin "not fair and not honest"
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in a phone interview on Friday that President Trump's decision to unilaterally lift sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel was "not fair and not honest."

  • "You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible," Zelensky said in frustration, referring to the Russian president's birthday earlier this week.

Why it matters: Trump's announcement, which came after a call with Putin, shocked Ukraine and many European governments and created a new crisis between the U.S. and its Western allies.

  • During the 15-minute interview, Zelensky sounded exasperated and dismayed and even expressed a sense of betrayal by the news of the diesel deal.
  • Trump was asked several times by reporters on Friday about Zelensky's criticism but declined to comment and said he was happy about the deal with Putin.

Driving the news: Trump announced the deal with Putin as his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting in Miami with the Ukrainian negotiating team along with senior diplomats from Germany, France, the U.K., the EU and NATO to discuss new U.S. ideas for ending the war.

  • Zelensky said he spoke several days ago with Witkoff about the need to continue efforts to reach a diplomatic breakthrough before winter and the midterm elections.
  • "Steve proposed to meet in Florida. And of course I accepted to go there and speak about the possibilities of negotiations. The Americans said they have some ideas and we agreed to come to discuss," Zelensky said.
  • At no point during his talks with Witkoff and Kushner did the U.S. suggest that a diesel deal with Russia was on the table, Zelensky stressed.
  • He said he understood from Witkoff that the U.S. envoys planned to take messages from the Florida talks to the Russians and then potentially travel to Kyiv to try to seal a peace deal.

Behind the scenes: Zelensky said that an hour before Trump's statement, his negotiators, who were meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Florida, informed him that Trump planned to speak with Putin. They said an announcement regarding U.S. sanctions on Russia might be forthcoming, without elaborating.

  • "It's not honest, really, because we tried to build our relations in the best way," he said. "It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this."

What he's saying: The Ukrainian president said he would have supported easing sanctions on Russian energy if it was done in the context of a deal to halt attacks on energy facilities in Ukraine and Russia during the winter.

  • "If the price is energy ceasefire, this negotiation is good," Zelensky said. But he argued that Trump presumably would have announced such a breakthrough if Putin had agreed to it.
  • "What did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world," Zelensky said.
  • Zelensky compared the current deal to the Anchorage summit between Trump and Putin last year, which ended with the U.S. president agreeing to many of the Russian demands regarding the war in Ukraine without getting anything in return.
  • "It looks like Alaska No. 2," he said.

Between the lines: Despite his anger, Zelensky stopped short of saying the episode meant Washington could no longer mediate between Kyiv and Moscow.

  • "It's not simple. We need the Americans," he said. "We need the Americans to try to stop this war."
  • But he questioned whether rewarding Moscow without an apparent Russian concession would make further diplomacy more difficult.
  • "This decision will not help us in any way," Zelensky said. "But what is bad, I think that this decision will not help Americans."

What's next: Zelensky said he plans to speak with his negotiating team to get a full readout of its talks with Witkoff and Kushner.

  • Zelensky said he also wanted to understand whether the diesel agreement was connected to a trip Trump's envoys planned to take to Russia.
  • "If you allow them to export diesel, and you think before that you have to go to Russia to negotiate, it looks that you are buying this meeting," Zelensky said, while stressing that he did not know whether that was actually Trump's intention.
  • "Maybe I'm not right," Zelensky said. "But it looks this way. Otherwise, why do it?"

item.title: Katie Zacharia tapped as next White House press secretary
item.description:
Katie Zacharia, a former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, will be the next White House press secretary, President Trump said Friday.

The big picture: Zacharia will take over the podium from Karoline Leavitt, a Trump loyalist who announced her departure from the administration in August.

What they're saying: "It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • "She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!"
  • "I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration."

Zoom in: Zacharia thanked Trump for the appointment in a Friday post on X.

  • "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime. President Trump has shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day," she wrote.
  • "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out. Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting."

Catch up quick: Zacharia is a conservative lawyer and commentator who works as a senior communications adviser at Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates Truth Social.

  • She also served for about six weeks as the Department of Homeland Security's deputy assistant secretary for public affairs and spokesperson. Zacharia announced her departure from DHS on March 31 in a post on X, saying she hoped to continue supporting the president's agenda "in other capacities."
  • Zacharia has worked as a commentator on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets.
  • She holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, where she currently serves on the school's Dean's Council.

The intrigue: Zacharia is less well-known than some of her predecessors, but she is a vocal defender of the administration on TV and online.

  • Trump also noted Friday that Zacharia had been involved in his 2024 presidential campaign, "assisting in key Swing States."
  • She also previously worked for Trump ally Richard Grenell at Fix California, an advocacy group that works to advance conservative values in the state. Zacharia has previously described herself as a "native Californian and lifelong conservative."
  • She told CNN in April that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol" and praised border czar Tom Homan's work on immigration.

Axios' Avery Lotz contributed to this reporting.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: Chuck Schumer has a 2028 problem that's not even in New York
item.description:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is going to have his hands full next Congress, even without a threat to his leadership or a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.).

Why it matters: Schumer (D-N.Y.) will have to grapple with the presidential ambitions of up to eight of his senators who may care more about winning the White House than following their leader.

  • Roughly one in six Democratic senators eyeing the campaign trail would add a degree of difficulty to a job that rarely lacks challenges, as former President Obama acknowledged this week.
  • "Being the head of the Democratic Party is a pain in the butt, because you've got people from every walk of life," Obama said of Schumer at a fundraiser Wednesday.

Flashback: This year's ICE funding fights gave Schumer a taste of how presidential ambitions can complicate governing.

  • Potential 2028 contenders competed to take the toughest stance against ICE funding, even at the risk of a government shutdown.

Zoom in: The tension between individual ambition and party unity could surface early in Schumer's tenure if he becomes majority leader.

  • Democrats are promising to lower costs and govern responsibly, while insisting they'll challenge and investigate the Trump administration at every turn.
  • Schumer and President Trump have a long, complicated relationship — and each other's cell numbers.

Between the lines: Democrats could control majorities in both chambers, giving them immense power against Trump.

  • But majority power is dependent on members being present and unified.
  • Presidential contenders have incentives to spend time outside Washington and show how they differ from their fellow 2028 hopefuls in the Senate.
  • They also may want to pick high-profile fights with the party establishment to prove their progressive bona fides.

But Schumer faced a similar challenge during the 2020 presidential cycle, when he was minority leader and seven sitting senators sought the Democratic nomination.

  • Attendance was the biggest headache as candidates crisscrossed the country, complicating Senate scheduling.
  • But Democrats didn't lose any major votes despite their presidential hopefuls being on the campaign trail.

Who we're watching:

  • Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) has visited South Carolina, New Hampshire and Nevada (twice).
  • Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.): South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa.
  • Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.): South Carolina (twice), Nevada and Michigan.
  • Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.): South Carolina, New Hampshire and Michigan.
  • Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.): Iowa and Nevada.
  • Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.): Iowa and New Hampshire (twice).
  • Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.): Nevada (twice) and New Hampshire.

Honorable mention: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is focused on winning reelection, so he has no documented early-primary-state visits yet. That hasn't stopped presidential rumors from swirling.

Zoom out: First, Schumer needs to get to at least 51 seats in November, navigate a high-stakes lame-duck session, and then win a secret-ballot election to reclaim his title as majority leader.

  • Some of his potential new members — especially if Democrats have a good night on Nov. 3 — aren't overly enthusiastic about supporting him.
  • Candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas have not committed to voting for him.

The bottom line: Presidential candidates want to stand out. Senate majority leaders need their members to blend in — and fall in line.

item.title: Trump announces major diesel deal with Putin, infuriating Ukraine
item.description:
President Trump announced Friday that he's reached a deal with Russia to increase the supply of diesel to the U.S. and global markets — angering Ukraine, which called it a gift to Vladimir Putin in the midst of their war.

Why it matters: The announcement, which includes a waiver on some U.S. energy sanctions against Russia, took place as Ukrainian and European diplomats arrived in Miami for talks on ending the war with Russia.

What he's saying: "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • Trump added that Russia will deliver," within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel."
  • Combine with oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, Trump wrote, "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"
  • "Today, at President Trump's direction, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market," the Treasury Department said in a statement.

Friction point: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky responded angrily to Trump's announcement, writing on X that any sanctions relief for Russia outside of a "lasting de-escalation agreement ... is an obvious weakness."

  • "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will repay the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," Zelensky wrote.
  • Zelensky added that Ukraine told Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff that it is "ready to take symmetrical de-escalatory steps" with Russia.
  • "Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure. This is the kind of agreement we are proposing to America, and we believe the U.S. has enough power to achieve such a compromise," he said.

The other side: The Kremlin said in a statement that during Putin's call with Trump, "significant attention was devoted to prospects for resolving the Ukraine crisis."

  • The Kremlin said the two leaders discussed the situation in global energy markets. "The Russian side confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the U.S. and global markets. I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the global economy as a whole," Putin said during the call, according to the Kremlin.
  • Putin special envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who worked on the deal, wrote on X that "Russia-US energy and economic cooperation will continue and benefit global markets and the world."

By the numbers: Ukrainian strikes cut Russia's available refining capacity by as much as 60% over the summer, though the effect varies month to month, per an analysis by two Dallas Fed researchers this week.

  • Through a combination of Middle East refinery outages, shipping constraints, damaged Russian refineries and curtailed Chinese refining, the global fuels market has seen reduction of as much as 6 million to 8 million barrels per day of capacity since late spring, or up to 10% of global refining.

What they're saying: "Putin and others are trying to opportunistically shift blame for high diesel prices onto Ukraine, rather than the U.S.-Israel-Iran war devastating global supply chains," said Joseph Webster, an energy and geopolitics analyst with the Atlantic Council, a nonpartisan think tank.

  • "These putative Russian export volumes are not only uncertain to materialize but are small in volume and wouldn't address the global diesel shortage," he said via email.

Ben Geman contributed to this report.

What they're saying: "Putin and others are trying to opportunistically shift blame for high diesel prices onto Ukraine, rather than the U.S.-Israel-Iran war devastating global supply chains," said Joseph Webster, an energy and geopolitics analyst with the Atlantic Council, a nonpartisan think tank.

  • "These putative Russian export volumes are not only uncertain to materialize but are small in volume and wouldn't address the global diesel shortage," he said via email.

Ben Geman contributed to this report.

item.title: DHS faces blowback over its attack on a Democratic House candidate
item.description:
The Department of Homeland Security is coming under fire for publicly attacking Democratic congressional candidate Janelle Stelson less than a month before the midterm election.

Why it matters: The Stelson campaign is threatening a lawsuit over the allegations, while a watchdog group is seeking an investigation into whether an ICE official violated restrictions on partisan political activity by federal employees.

  • "We are likely to take legal action to combat the blatant lies and coordinated misinformation campaign," Stelson campaign manager Alma Baker said in a statement to Axios.
  • The campaign said Friday it has sent out cease and desist letters, viewed by Axios, to several news outlets that reported DHS's claims as fact.
  • The race between Stelson and Republican Rep. Scott Perry in Pennsylvania's 10th district is one of the most competitive and expensive House elections in the country, attracting more than $26 million in spending, according to AdImpact.

Driving the news: DHS published a press release on Wednesday announcing the arrest of what it said was an "illegal alien from Nigeria who exposed himself in public while working for congressional campaign in Pennsylvania."

  • The migrant, Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe, was arrested by ICE on Oct. 1 after pleading guilty to disorderly conduct last month, according to the press release.
  • The release included a statement from ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall saying: "It's unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a Congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public."

Stelson herself quickly batted down the claim: "He's not an employee. He's not a volunteer," she said at an event on Wednesday.

  • Nobody named Igbojekwe was paid by the Stelson campaign as of Sept. 30, according to disbursements tracked by the Federal Election Commission. The campaign also showed Axios a search of its volunteer database that turned up no results for the name.
  • In its cease-and-desist letter, the campaign said Igbojekwe has also "never been employed by any vendors of the campaign."
  • Asked Thursday for comment on this story, DHS sent Axios its initial press release. The agency did not respond to multiple follow-up emails requesting comment on the Stelson campaign's threat of legal action.

Between the lines: DHS cited a New Jersey-based news outlet called "Shore News Network" as its source for the claim that Igbojekwe was a Stelson canvasser. That outlet cited a social media post from conservative activist Scott Presler.

  • "A canvasser for democrat Janelle Stelson ... was reportedly charged for indecent exposure," Presler wrote in a post on X, which included a photo of a court document that did not make reference to the Stelson campaign.
  • Presler did not respond to a request for comment from Axios.

Axios obtained an affidavit in which Trevor Jeffers, the East Pennsboro, Pa., police officer who made the initial arrest, testified that Igbojekwe was sitting in a parked car in a residential neighborhood "wearing nothing but a shirt" with his "genitals ... exposed."

  • "Igbojekwe advised that he was in the neighborhood for work and that he was waiting to hand out flyers for Janelle Stelson's political campaign," Jeffers said in the affidavit, adding that Igbojekwe "was able to provide a stack of flyers showing he was there for work."
  • The East Pennsboro Police did not provide a comment and denied Axios' public records request for documents related to the case.
  • Several news outlets that covered the initial arrest or the DHS press release have since deleted their stories and posts. None responded to Axios' requests for comment.
  • The Stelson campaign, asked about the affidavit, referred Axios to Baker's statement on Wednesday saying Igbojekwe had "never been employed" by them and that they had "never heard of him prior to the news of his arrest."

Zoom in: Igbojekwe was charged with indecent exposure and disorderly conduct, later pleading guilty to a single count of disorderly conduct, according to court records.

  • The attorney listed as his representative in court documents, Cumberland County first assistant public defender Arla Waller, did not return multiple phone calls seeking comment.
  • Igbojekwe did not respond to a request for comment sent to an email address listed under his name.

The latest: The Office of Special Counsel "will open a file" in response to questions about whether Wall violated the Hatch Act, which prohibits mixing federal government work with political campaigning, according to emails shared with Axios.

  • Donald Sherman, the executive director of ethics watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, wrote in an email to OSC that Wall's statement was "gratuitous partisanship that constitutes prohibited political activity."
  • An OSC staffer replied to Sherman: "We received your complaint and will open a file to address this matter."
  • An OSC spokesperson confirmed the authenticity of the emails but declined to comment further. Wall did not respond to a request for comment.

What they're saying: Deborah Fleischaker, a former acting ICE chief of staff under the Biden administration, told Axios that legal counsel at the agency during her tenure "almost certainly would have recommended not to say something like" what Wall did in his statement.

  • Directly referencing an election in an official statement "really is seen as a no no," she told Axios.
  • Fleischaker acknowledged that federal ethics rules aren't the deterrent they used to be.

The bottom line: Cook Political Report rates the race between Stelson and Perry for the Harrisburg-based House seat as a toss-up.

  • The Freedom Caucus Fund, a hybrid PAC dedicated to electing and supporting House Freedom Caucus members, released a digital ad on Thursday calling Igbojekwe a "Nigerian illegal alien campaigning for Democrat Janelle Stelson."

item.title: The surprising post-pandemic drop in income inequality
item.description:
Data: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Middle- and lower-earners' inflation-adjusted incomes rose during the Biden years — but high earners saw their incomes fall.

  • That's a surprising finding from one of the most thorough datasets on American household finances, released Friday morning by the Federal Reserve.

Why it matters: The data sheds granular new information on a much-contested question: What happened to Americans' real incomes during the post-pandemic period? It featured an exceptionally tight job market and the highest inflation in decades, followed by aggressive Fed rate hikes.

  • The median American family's income rose 7% in inflation-adjusted terms between 2021 and 2024. But that masked significant differences among income brackets.
  • The average real income of families in the top 10% of earners fell 14%, to $652,000 from $757,000 (both figures are 2025 dollars).
  • That implies, contrary to a common narrative about the K-shaped economy, that income inequality fell during the post-pandemic period.

Yes, but: The story for wealth is very different. Families that were already wealthy — and tend to own stocks, houses and other assets — became much richer from 2022 to 2025.

  • Among families in the top 10% of income, median net worth rose a whopping 31% from 2022 to 2025, compared with a 2% rise in net worth for the median family.
  • Families in the bottom 40% of income actually saw their net worth decline slightly in that span.

The intrigue: The data, from the Survey of Consumer Finances, is collected and released every three years. Friday morning's release is the 2025 survey — but questions about income cover the preceding calendar year.

  • As such, the income numbers compare 2024 with 2021 — conveniently capturing the change from the early part of the Biden administration to near its end.

Between the lines: While the compression in income inequality seen in this data may seem surprising, it aligns with other evidence that blue-collar workers saw bigger raises during the super-tight job market and inflationary episode of 2021 and 2022 than did higher-earning white-collar professionals.

  • Moreover, in a footnote, the Fed researchers note that top earners tend to have income from volatile sources, mainly capital gains and business income.
  • Big swings in those income sources among the highest earners can create outsized movement in the averages.

Of note: The survey also sheds light on how the Fed's aggressive interest rate hikes in 2022 and 2023, meant to bring inflation under control, hammered borrowers.

  • The median debt payment-to-income ratio rose 2 percentage points from 2022 to 2025, reaching 15.4%.
  • The share of families with debt payment-to-income ratios above 40%, a threshold for high debt obligations, increased to 8.6% from 6.5%, reaching a level last seen in the 2013 survey.

The bottom line: Low earners saw bigger percentage gains in their incomes' purchasing power amid the post-pandemic inflation than did high earners — but the rich got a lot richer at the same time.

item.title: Cook Political Report tilts 18 House races toward Democrats
item.description:
House races in Iowa, Pennsylvania, Washington, Michigan and more are shifting in Democrats' direction, according to a Friday update from the closely watched Cook Political Report.

Why it matters: The GOP's midterm outlook was already bleak, anchored by an unpopular war and high fuel prices. But staving off a blue resurgence, despite heavy spending, is looking increasingly complicated as Election Day approaches.

Driving the news: Cook's new moves put the likely midterm outcome at Democrats picking up nine to 19 seats, a range of 224 to 234. The shifts include:

  • Five seats — in Iowa, Pennsylvania and Washington — moving from toss ups to leaning toward Democrats, including Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' (R-Iowa) tough rematch race against Democrat ⁠Christina Bohannan.
  • Cook also nudged four races  — in Iowa, Michigan, North Carolina and Virginia — from leaning toward Republicans to toss-ups. That's good news for Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.), whose district was warped by mid-decade redistricting.
  • Republicans' hold on other races in Kentucky, Maine, Pennsylvania, Arkansas and Indiana slipped, shifting them to Lean R or Likely R. Meanwhile, Democrats' hold on Nevada, New York and Nebraska races tightened.

What they're saying: "House races are won in the districts, one by one, with battle-tested candidates and messages that work," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella said in a statement provided to Axios.

  • "Pundits in D.C. can keep guessing, but voters on the ground have a clear contrast between common sense and crazy," he said, adding that "in November, we're going to win."

Friction point: President Trump is crisscrossing the country to campaign for GOP candidates. But with the midterms serving as a referendum on his White House, his polling may well be a liability for Republicans in tight races.

  • Republicans have quietly distanced themselves from the president — and it appears even some Trump voters get it: A Politico poll out Friday found that some one-in-four who voted for him in 2024 say the Republican candidate in their district would be better off breaking from Trump.

Zoom in: Of the seats labeled "Toss Up" by Cook, six are held by Democrats, and 15 belong to Republicans.

  • Per Cook, Democrats need to win 20% of the toss-up races to reach a majority, assuming the seats that favor them in the nonpartisan analysis go Democrats' way.

The bottom line: The political environment keeps deteriorating for Republicans, even after the dust cleared from the redistricting battle and with their financial advantage.

Go deeper: House GOP leaders admit redistricting fell short

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a response from the NRCC.

item.title: Navi Pillay, advocate for international law, wins Nobel Peace Prize
item.description:
Navi Pillay, an outspoken supporter of international law who has served as a judge on multiple global courts and as the UN's top human rights official, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday.

Why it matters: President Trump once again did not win the prize he has openly coveted.

  • Pillay, among other posts, previously served on the International Criminal Court — a body Trump sanctioned and last month called "rogue" and "evil."

What they're saying: "The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order," the prize committee said in a social media post.

  • "This year's laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted."

Background: Besides the ICC and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, Pillay also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

  • Pillay, 85 and a native of South Africa, began practicing law in the late 1960s and served on her country's high court before her international appointments.

Zoom out: Pillay stands for many of the ideas and institutions Trump has condemned.

  • Besides sanctioning the ICC, he withdrew the U.S. from the UN Human Rights Council last year.
  • He's also made a target of South Africa and its Black government, promising asylum to white South African farmers.
  • The AP reported that Pillay, reacting to the news, said world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war."

The big picture: The Nobel Peace Prize is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about constantly and has frequently insisted he should have won.

  • Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, gave Trump her prize medal earlier this year — though the Norwegian Nobel Institute made clear the prize itself could not actually be transferred.

The intrigue: As of mid-morning Friday, Trump hadn't reacted publicly to the news — but he did repost a Truth Social post condemning Pillay and praising his accomplishments as a better choice for the prize.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with Trump's reaction.

item.title: How the permitting bill could collapse
item.description:
Congress has its best chance in years to pass sweeping permitting legislation, but a series of political and policy obstacles could derail the bipartisan Senate plan.

Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors, and major business groups more broadly.

Here are five risks to a lame-duck deal:

👱‍♂️ President Trump himself. The White House says it supports the bill, but Trump is mercurial, so nothing is final until it's final.

  • His administration's willingness — or not — to loosen the screws on wind and solar projects it's restricting could also sway the lame-duck politics and complicate efforts to win Democratic support.
  • Flashback: Co-author Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) last month cited "unresolved" questions about Trump officials returning to "regular order" for renewables, but credited their "very reasonable" proposal.

🗳️ A big blue wave. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), a senior House Democrat, has been arguing that Democrats will have more leverage next year.

  • For now, there's little evidence that view is gaining traction among Democrats. The few definitive statements on the bill from lawmakers in both parties are supportive. But a strong Democratic showing in November could change that calculation.
  • The big arguments against waiting: Dems won't have 60 votes even if they take the Senate, and Trump still needs to sign anything, limiting the prospects for a better deal next year.

🟩 Environmentalists. Groups with close ties to Dems — such as the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Evergreen Action — are still weighing their positions on the bill.

  • A coordinated push against it could make it harder for Democratic lawmakers to back the legislation.

⚡ Utilities. Regulated utilities would see new competition in transmission development and greater oversight of their planning and business.

  • American Electric Power and Berkshire Hathaway Energy support the bill, but the sector's trade group — the Edison Electric Institute — has not taken a position.

⏰ The lame-duck squeeze. A busy legislative calendar, potential changes to the bill and uncertainty about lawmakers' appetite for legislating after the election could leave too little time to secure passage through both chambers.

  • Already, House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) told Punchbowl News that he wants to modify the electricity provisions.
  • If Republicans lose the House majority, their willingness to push a major bipartisan deal across the finish line could diminish.
  • "It's hard to convince people to hang around and wait for something to happen when they're being constantly reminded that they lost," Jeff Navin, a former Democratic Hill staffer and co-founder of clean tech lobbying firm Boundary Stone Partners, said via email.

The bottom line: This is a partial list!

  • To riff on Mickey Rourke's advice to William Hurt in the great 1981 noir flick "Body Heat," there are 50 ways to mess up any bill, and if you can think of 25, you're a genius.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

  • Already, House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) told Punchbowl News that he wants to modify the electricity provisions.
  • If Republicans lose the House majority, their willingness to push a major bipartisan deal across the finish line could diminish.
  • "It's hard to convince people to hang around and wait for something to happen when they're being constantly reminded that they lost," Jeff Navin, a former Democratic Hill staffer and co-founder of clean tech lobbying firm Boundary Stone Partners, said via email.

The bottom line: This is a partial list!

  • To riff on Mickey Rourke's advice to William Hurt in the great 1981 noir flick "Body Heat," there are 50 ways to mess up any bill, and if you can think of 25, you're a genius.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: AI vs. the rest of the economy
item.description:
Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: Data center construction includes construction costs, such as labor, materials, profits of contractors, architectural and engineering work and miscellaneous overhead, interest and taxes. Does not include servers, racks, chips or memory.

More and more, it seems as if there's the AI economy — and everything else.

Why it matters: The growing chasm between the breakneck growth of the AI world and the slower pace of the economy where most Americans work and live has huge implications, especially for the markets.

Zoom in: The most recent numbers on U.S. construction spending through August — shown above — paint the picture remarkably clearly.

Zoom out: The same divide is an important theme in the markets as well.

  • In corporate bonds, AI-related offerings accounted for more than half of net investment grade issuance for the year through the end of August, according to data from Apollo and Bloomberg.
Data: Apollo, Bloomberg; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

And of course, excitement over all things related to AI has supercharged the market values of Nvidia, the hyperscalers and other AI-related tech stocks.

Stunning stat: The weighting of the S&P 500 technology sector in terms of market capitalization is now roughly 40%. That's higher than during the peak of the dot-com bubble.

  • But that actually underplays the impact of AI.
  • If you throw in the hyperscalers Meta and Amazon, which S&P doesn't include in the tech sector, the share of the AI-pilled part of the blue-chip index climbs closer to 50%.
Data: FactSet, Axios; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

The bottom line: The growth gap between AI and everything else means the U.S. economy and the markets are increasingly yoked to AI — and all the risks that come with it.

item.title: Scoop: AI companies plot "day after" scenarios for public revolt
item.description:
Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies are privately gaming out scenarios for a public and political revolt after a catastrophic AI event.

Why it matters: These officials anticipate a large-scale event, most likely a cyberattack, that shuts down access to financial services, internet connectivity, or even power and water.

  • The first example of significant real-world harm caused by unsafe AI would turn an already wary public further against the technology and its leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, as well as President Trump for his reluctance to regulate it.

Threat level: While scenario planning is common within many companies and national security settings — the Pentagon has been running war games for decades — the difference is that many top AI researchers and executives believe a major incident is inevitable.

  • "OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," a company spokesperson said. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable, but are meant to help us prepare for a variety of circumstances."
  • Anthropic declined to comment.

Zoom in: The blame game will start whether a rogue-agent swarm breaks containment from an internal testing environment or a bad actor finds unexpected ways to use available models.

  • A recent campaign targeting South Korean financial organizations — including reported breaches at two banks — shows the damage one person can do.
  • A hacker from China allegedly used AI tools from China-developed models, including DeepSeek, to steal data from tens of thousands of bank customers. The attacker used Claude Code to ask for help finding places to sell the stolen data, according to cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike.

Top AI planners assume Democrats, ascendant after the midterms, will move fast to shut down AI but will face significant challenges.

  • An aging Congress, out of touch with the AI revolution, could find itself out of its depth.
  • The global economy is now heavily intertwined with an AI infrastructure buildout. Slowing it down could hit an already fragile economy hard.
  • Too many open-weight models can already be freely downloaded and used to cause harm, a problem most cybersecurity pros see as solvable only by using AI to fight rogue AI.

Between the lines: The planning involves red-teaming for worst-case scenarios. It focuses mainly on racing to educate members of Congress.

  • Company executives know regulation has no chance of passing right now, but still want to shape the legislation and policies U.S. leaders will turn to after a first catastrophic event.

What we're watching: Many AI industry insiders told Axios they believe a major event will occur in the next six to 12 months.

  • Even with Democrats in control of the House and Senate, the companies see fractured politics as the norm, including within the Democratic Party.
  • Some of the most heavy-handed Democratic proposals include banning superintelligence or pausing advanced AI development.
  • Others have bipartisan support and even some industry buy-in, including a required kill switch on advanced AI. But experts have questioned the viability of trying to turn off all AI systems.

The bottom line: In a real crisis, Washington can set partisan differences aside. One Democratic aide pointed to cooperation during COVID and the 2008 financial crisis.

item.title: Immigration split screen: Microsoft gets a crackdown and a medal
item.description:
The Trump administration said Thursday that it was suspending Microsoft from a key program used to sponsor employees for green cards. Later that day, the administration honored the tech giant's CEO with a medal for innovation.

Why it matters: The split-screen day highlights the tension between the administration's championing of Big Tech and its immigration policies, which constrain an industry that has long relied on hiring foreign-born workers.

  • Tech leaders have said that restrictions on hiring hamper the country's ability to compete — especially at a moment when the U.S. is in a race with China on AI.

Driving the news: The administration's move Thursday also targeted Adobe and six IT services firms over the Permanent Employment Program, or Perm.

  • It's typically the first major government approval step in employers sponsoring workers, often H-1B holders, for employment-based green cards.
  • The administration accused these companies of hiring foreign workers and paying them less, at U.S. workers' expense.

State of play: President Trump awarded Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House's New Golden Age Summit Thursday night.

  • Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google co-founder Sergey Brin and CEO of AMD Lisa Su — like Nadella, all immigrants to the U.S. — were awarded the National Medal of Science.
  • At the event, Trump called the honorees "national treasures."

What they're saying: Vice President Vance addressed the apparent contradiction at a press conference earlier Thursday, saying: "Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company; it's that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans."

  • Microsoft "laid off 6,000 American workers while replacing them with 6,300 H-1Bs," he said.
  • Vance didn't provide a timeline. "The suspension of Perm is going to last as long as it needs to," he said. "We have a number of tools to suspend it indefinitely."

The other side: Microsoft said in a statement Thursday that 80% of the applications it submitted in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees — not to hire new people.

  • "We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings."
  • It didn't directly address the Perm program.

Zoom in: The Department of Labor said it won't accept new Perm applications from the eight companies it named nor would it process those already in the pipeline.

  • This is a process that can already take years for some workers — and many are long-time trusted employees inside those companies.

By the numbers: In fiscal year 2025, the Labor Department certified nearly 140,000 of these Perm applications, and nearly 118,000 new ones were filed — down 22% from the previous year.

  • Roughly 30% of certified applications were for software developers, computer systems analysts and data scientists.
  • Microsoft's stock price fell about 1% after the news, but overall investors didn't seem flustered. Adobe shares rose nearly 4%.

What to watch: Lawyers say the move could make companies more reluctant to sponsor workers for visas and permanent residency. And it could turn off talented foreign workers and students from coming to the U.S.

  • The Perm program is "a fundamental way of getting a green card in the U.S. for workers," says Patricia Gannon, chair of the Immigration and Naturalization Group and the law firm Greenspoon Marder.
  • "It's going to make foreign workers more hesitant to accept positions in the United States," says Hiba Anver, an attorney at Erickson Immigration Group. "I have concerns about a shrinking talent pool in the United States."

Catch up quick: This isn't the administration's first effort on the H-1B labor force.

  • In September 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced a $100,000 fee on H-1B visas.
  • Roughly five months later, just 85 people had paid the fee, according to a court filing.
  • Numerous federal judges have now struck down the fee.

Brittany Gibson contributed reporting.

item.title: "Not a fetish, not a taboo": Democrats weigh another Trump impeachment
item.description:
Democrats believe President Trump has committed impeachable offenses. But they're divided over whether they should try to impeach him if they win control of the House.

Why it matters: If Democrats win the House, as expected, their 2027 decision on whether to try to impeach Trump could have major consequences for the 2028 presidential race.

Zoom in: Theoretically, impeaching Trump would be easy for a unified, Democrat-controlled House.

  • Many top Democrats note that Trump survived a record two impeachments in his first term — and that he'd be unlikely to be removed from office. That would require a two-thirds, bipartisan vote in a Senate that's likely to be closely divided.
  • Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said Trump has "already committed numerous impeachable offenses" in his second term, including usurping congressional authority. In 2021, Raskin led the second Trump impeachment, following the Jan. 6 Capitol riot.
  • Raskin said top Democrats are "very sober about what that two-thirds requirement means on the Senate side. If anything, Donald Trump has tightened his control over the Republican Party since the last round. He's gotten rid of the senators that he viewed as not sufficiently loyal and sycophantic."

Zoom out: Other Democrats also are cautioning against an impeachment campaign if their party takes control of the House in January.

  • Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a potential presidential candidate, told NBC's "Meet the Press" last Sunday that he supports investigations, not impeachment, "because it's not going anywhere and it's going to be a food fight."
  • Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) said recently: "Don't be impeaching anybody ... Let's just get back to work."

Friction point: Democrats' more progressive wing is already talking about an impeachment drive.

  • Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told The Floridian in March: "If you are asking me if I support impeachment, I do. I think that it's on very objective grounds of following the law or not."
  • Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a liberal who, like AOC, is weighing a White House run, also has argued for impeachment.
  • "It's about setting a standard," he told NBC News, rejecting the notion that an impeachment would distract Democrats from pushing policy changes. "Democrats can impeach to uphold constitutional values, and at the same time have a first-hundred-day agenda that deals with the cost of living."

What's next: Trump, who denies wrongdoing, is already preparing for his third impeachment. He told reporters Wednesday that he was "never even worried" about his first two impeachments.

  • "I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump said, calling the impeachments and subsequent criminal cases against him "very illegal things."
  • "I view the presidency as a very sacred position," he said. "Very sacred position. Very important. Very sacred. A position where it has to be treated properly."

Deep down, Trump might welcome an impeachment, one adviser said, "because he's in his element in chaos and when he's being persecuted."

  • A longtime confidant said: "If Democrats win and start the investigations, he'll get more defiant ... Democrats won't be able to resist impeachment and he won't be able to resist daring them to do it. You think you control Donald Trump? Well, f*ck you. You don't."
  • A senior administration official said the belief within the White House is that an impeachment would "just prove Democrats are all about getting Trump, and this stuff about affordability is just a hoax."

Between the lines: Democrats know they face a conflict between holding Trump accountable and delivering on their campaign promises to restore Medicaid cuts and bolster the Affordable Care Act.

  • Raskin said: "Does this make sense as a matter of law and politics and public policy to advance another impeachment? That's obviously a more complex question than whether or not he's violating the Constitution when he goes to war without congressional consent or he imposes tariffs outside of the law, or he engages in unprecedented scales of corruption in abusing his office."
  • "So all this is to say, it is not a fetish with us," he added. "On the other hand, it's definitely not a taboo."

Raskin, a law professor, is in line to lead the House Judiciary Committee, which would be involved in any impeachment. He emphasizes that "impeachment is by definition an intertwined question of both law and politics."

  • In other words, it's not just a legal process.
  • That's why the House impeaches and the president is then tried in the Senate, not the Supreme Court.

The intrigue: Some Democrats have been at odds with themselves on impeachment.

  • Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), another potential 2028 candidate, said in April 2025 that he "strongly" supported impeaching Trump and that there's "no question" the president committed impeachable offenses.
  • By this summer, however, Ossoff was no longer committed to it.

Behind the scenes: Some Republicans have indicated that if they keep control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 election, they could bypass an impeachment trial by simply voting to dismiss the charges.

  • Senate Democrats did that in 2024, after President Biden's homeland security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by the House. Senate Republican leaders warned then that Democrats were setting a precedent they may not like when Republicans were in charge.

Then there's Vice President Vance. He's likely to run for president over the next two years as Democrats debate impeachment.

  • "JD relishes nothing more than defending the president," an administration official said. "More 'lawfare' against POTUS will unify Republicans even more."
  • "If Democrats want JD to become president, please, impeach Trump."

item.title: California threatens to worsen House Democrats' 2027 headaches
item.description:
More than half a dozen U.S. House districts in California will send a Democrat to Capitol Hill next year no matter what. Party leadership still has a lot riding on the outcome.

Why it matters: Most of these Democrat vs. Democrat runoffs — a quirk of California's election system — are between an establishment candidate and an outsider vowing to make leadership's life hell.

  • Democratic Reps. Mike Thompson, Doris Matsui and Jimmy Gomez are all facing well-funded challenges from younger, less establishment-aligned Democrats.
  • There are also several Northern California races that feature a pro-leadership Democrat facing off against a more left-leaning rival.
  • Sought for comment on this story, Justin Chermol, a spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), told Axios: "Stop wasting our time with your irrelevant stories that have nothing to do with taking back control of the House of Representatives."

4th District: Rep. Mike Thompson vs. Eric Jones

Thompson, a 75-year-old first elected in 1998, faces a challenge from 35-year-old former venture capitalist Eric Jones.

  • "I don't think anyone in Democratic leadership today is really doing their job well," Jones said in an interview with Axios.
  • Asked if he would vote for Jeffries as speaker, Jones replied: "As of today, I wouldn't vote for any member."

Jones is trying to cobble together a populist, anti-establishment coalition consisting of both progressives and Republicans. He said he does not identify as progressive, telling Axios he prefers "no labels."

  • He said that, if elected, he will "have the benefit of independence ... of not taking party money, and I'm not going to vote a party line."

7th District: Rep. Doris Matsui vs. Mai Vang

Matsui, 82, is seen as particularly vulnerable after finishing second to Mai Vang in the jungle primary election in June.

  • Vang, a progressive Sacramento City Councilmember in her 40s, has positioned herself alongside a new bloc of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-aligned candidates including Darializa Avila Chevalier, Chris Rabb and Melat Kiros.
  • She previously signaled to Axios she won't vote for Jeffries as speaker, saying she "cannot support this kind of leadership" and that "we need new leadership and a new direction."

11th District: Scott Wiener vs. Connie Chan

The fight between state Sen. Scott Wiener and San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan to succeed former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has been particularly bitter.

  • Chan has positioned herself to the left of Wiener, a longtime progressive who has come under fire from the pro-Palestinian movement for being insufficiently critical of Israel.
  • Wiener told Mission Local he looks "forward to electing Hakeem Jeffries speaker."
  • Chan told the outlet that "any candidate for speaker, including Hakeem Jeffries, will have to earn my vote."

14th District: Rep. Aisha Wahab vs. Melissa Hernandez

Wahab, a progressive former state senator, defeated Hernandez, the more moderate former mayor of Dublin, California, in an August special election to replace former Rep. Eric Swalwell.

  • The two are now duking it out for a full term.
  • Wahab has already shown her willingness to buck leadership: She defied Pelosi and Jeffries by running in the special election instead of allowing a "caretaker" to run unopposed, according to The Sunday Times.
  • The Wahab and Hernandez campaigns did not respond to questions about whether their candidates would vote for Jeffries as speaker.

34th District: Rep. Jimmy Gomez vs. Angela Gonzales-Torres

Gomez has come under fire after the House Ethics Committee opened an investigation into him in August over allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies.

  • He has been a longtime target of the left, having survived three consecutive primary challenges from Democrat David Kim since 2020 by 2 to 11 percentage points.
  • This time he faces a challenge from Angela Gonzales-Torres, a progressive local neighborhood councilor backed by many of the same left-wing groups that support Vang and Wahab.

Gonzales-Torres, asked in an interview with Axios if she would vote for Jeffries as speaker, said she looks forward to "supporting leaders who are not nearly funded by corporate super PACs."

  • Gonzales-Torres, pointing to her support from DSA, said she considers herself part of the "national slate" of progressive insurgents such as Avila Chevalier, Rabb and Kiros.
  • "Right now [what] we are focusing on is winning this election and hopefully getting to be part of utilizing our bargaining power as this incoming class in Congress," she said.

The bottom line: The larger the bloc of Jeffries skeptics that arrives on Capitol Hill in January, the worse a time Democratic leadership will have.

  • That could be tempered to a large degree by the size of Democrats' potential majority, but, as Axios previously reported, many red-seat candidates are also maintaining their independence from leadership.
  • Still, few Democrats think Jeffries will ultimately be denied the speakership. The fights that come after are more uncertain.

Editor's note: This article has been corrected to note Rep. Matsui is 82 (not 85).
item.content:encoded:
More than half a dozen U.S. House districts in California will send a Democrat to Capitol Hill next year no matter what. Party leadership still has a lot riding on the outcome.

Why it matters: Most of these Democrat vs. Democrat runoffs — a quirk of California's election system — are between an establishment candidate and an outsider vowing to make leadership's life hell.

  • Democratic Reps. Mike Thompson, Doris Matsui and Jimmy Gomez are all facing well-funded challenges from younger, less establishment-aligned Democrats.
  • There are also several Northern California races that feature a pro-leadership Democrat facing off against a more left-leaning rival.
  • Sought for comment on this story, Justin Chermol, a spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), told Axios: "Stop wasting our time with your irrelevant stories that have nothing to do with taking back control of the House of Representatives."

4th District: Rep. Mike Thompson vs. Eric Jones

Thompson, a 75-year-old first elected in 1998, faces a challenge from 35-year-old former venture capitalist Eric Jones.

  • "I don't think anyone in Democratic leadership today is really doing their job well," Jones said in an interview with Axios.
  • Asked if he would vote for Jeffries as speaker, Jones replied: "As of today, I wouldn't vote for any member."

Jones is trying to cobble together a populist, anti-establishment coalition consisting of both progressives and Republicans. He said he does not identify as progressive, telling Axios he prefers "no labels."

  • He said that, if elected, he will "have the benefit of independence ... of not taking party money, and I'm not going to vote a party line."

7th District: Rep. Doris Matsui vs. Mai Vang

Matsui, 82, is seen as particularly vulnerable after finishing second to Mai Vang in the jungle primary election in June.

  • Vang, a progressive Sacramento City Councilmember in her 40s, has positioned herself alongside a new bloc of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-aligned candidates including Darializa Avila Chevalier, Chris Rabb and Melat Kiros.
  • She previously signaled to Axios she won't vote for Jeffries as speaker, saying she "cannot support this kind of leadership" and that "we need new leadership and a new direction."

The fight between state Sen. Scott Wiener and San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan to succeed former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has been particularly bitter.

item.title: Kushner, Witkoff to pitch "new ideas" to end Russia-Ukraine war
item.description:
Presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet with Ukrainian negotiators and European officials in Miami on Friday to present "new ideas and proposals" to break the stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine war, U.S. and Ukrainian officials say.

Why it matters: The Trump administration is hoping to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the midterm elections and before brutal winter weather grips Ukraine.

  • One of the ideas is a partial ceasefire that halts attacks on energy infrastructure and grain shipments. While Ukraine has said it's willing to take that step, Russia has shown little willingness.
  • "They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop. So the U.S. is trying to mediate with the sides, with the goal of creating a unified proposal," a U.S. source said.

Driving the news: Witkoff and Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September. Since then, they've been working with the Russians and Ukrainians on an updated peace initiative.

  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at a press conference in Lisbon Thursday that the war is at a "stalemate." He stressed that the U.S. wants to prevent further escalation of fighting in the coming month and find a way to end the war.

Behind the scenes: Witkoff and Kushner met with President Trump Thursday to present the latest U.S. proposal and receive his input ahead of the talks in Miami, which are expected to last two days, a U.S. official said.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and deputy national security adviser Mike Needham also attended the meeting.

Zoom in: President Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, Foreign Intelligence director Rustem Umerov, diplomatic adviser Sergey Kyslytsia and Member of Parliament Davyd Arakhamia will participate from the Ukrainian side.

  • The U.S. also invited national security advisers from the U.K., France and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the EU.
  • A U.S. source said the parties will discuss proposals for security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war prosperity plan and other aspects of the conflict.

The other side: Zelensky told reporters on Thursday that Ukraine is discussing with the U.S. the possibility of an energy and grain ceasefire.

  • "As for what might be realistic or more realistic, I am not ready to say yet. I do not want to say something and then have Russia, as always, do the opposite out of spite. So let's wait and see," he said.

Between the lines: A Ukrainian official said that despite skepticism in Kyiv, the U.S. midterm elections and Russia's need for sanctions relief might lead Russian President Vladimir Putin to agree to a ceasefire of some sort.

What to watch: Witkoff and Kushner might travel to Moscow later this month for more talks with Putin, a source with knowledge said.

item.title: Pete Hegseth says the public can watch Fort Hood shooter's execution
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that the public will be able to watch the execution of the Fort Hood shooter by firing squad.

Why it matters: The U.S. hasn't held a public execution in 90 years, and Hegseth's remarks raise questions about how the military would allow people to watch.

  • Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, near Killeen, Texas.

What they're saying: Hegseth told Real America's Voice Thursday that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be."

  • "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it's public. Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."

The latest: The Pentagon says the execution will be livestreamed, AP reports, but did not name where specifically the stream will be hosted.

  • The Pentagon currently posts speeches and videos on X and YouTube.

State of play: The Department of Defense declined to comment on Hegseth's remarks, leaving questions about how the public could watch the execution.

  • The Army has not shared how it intends to conduct the execution, AP reports.
  • It's unclear if Hegseth's remarks mean the execution will be open to public spectators, broadcast on streaming or TV, or made available to select individuals.

Zoom out: This would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.

  • The last U.S. military execution by firing squad was in 1945, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, according to NPR.

Firing-squad executions are rare in the U.S.

  • Only Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah authorize the method, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
  • Last year, South Carolina carried out the state's first firing squad execution — the first in the U.S. in 15 years.
  • The last public execution in the U.S. was in 1936, when Rainey Bethea, a Black man convicted of raping a white woman, was hanged in Kentucky.

item.title: The staggering cost of winning a Senate seat in 2026
item.description:
Source: AdImpact, Census.gov Note: AdImpact data includes dollars spent on video advertisements on broadcast, cable and social media as well as spending estimates on streaming platforms. Chart: Stef Kight/Axios

Every voting-age Mainer could get a $167 voucher for home heating oil with what Democrats and Republicans are spending on ads in the Senate race, according to an analysis of AdImpact data.

Why it matters: Every senator gets one vote, but Senate seats aren't created equal — and they don't cost the same.

Zoom in: Like two years ago, the less-populated states have a dramatically higher dollar-per-voter ratio in 2026.

  • Maine is in first place, followed by Alaska, which is scheduled to be hit with $76 million in ads — enough to suck up most of the state's inventory.

Between the lines: Ohio is only in fifth place on the dollar-per-voter metric, but it's on track to host the most expensive Senate race in the country — for the second cycle in a row.

  • Sherrod Brown's comeback bid is proving more expensive than his 2024 race, when he was ousted by now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio).
  • And in New Hampshire, where Democratic Senate nominee Chris Pappas has been warning that his race is actually quite close, both parties are spending heavily to reach the state's voters.
Data: AdImpact Note: AdImpact data includes dollars spent on video advertisements on broadcast, cable and social media as well as spending estimates on streaming platforms. Chart: Stef Kight/Axios

The big picture: Both chambers are likely to come down to a handful of races.

  • All year, Republicans warned that Texas would get really expensive if Attorney General Ken Paxton won the primary. They were right.
  • Outside GOP groups spent a mind-blowing $131 million in just 17 days trying to rescue Paxton. And tens of millions more could be on the way.
  • But in North Carolina, where Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), predicted the race could cost $1 billion, the contest looks like it will come in under $200 million.
  • Republican super PACs are abandoning the Senate race there as they reallocate money to redder states.

The bottom line: Republicans have a spending advantage, especially when it comes to how many eyeballs they're actually reaching in Texas and Ohio.

  • But neither side has really figured out how to play moneyball and find a way to reach voters with a dramatically smaller budget.
