item.title: Exclusive: Anthropic's plan to protect critical infrastructure
item.description:
Anthropic is launching a new cybersecurity initiative designed to bring its most powerful AI models and engineers to companies protecting power grids, water utilities and other critical infrastructure, the company first shared with Axios.

Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are struggling to secure aging, complex systems as AI threatens to make cyberattacks faster and cheaper to execute.

Driving the news: Under its new Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, Anthropic will provide its frontier AI models, onsite engineers and threat research to companies already responsible for securing critical infrastructure systems.

  • Participating companies will use these resources to identify and fix vulnerabilities in their customers' systems.
  • The program's founding partners include Accenture, Booz Allen Hamilton, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC and Rockwell Automation.
  • Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same.

Zoom in: Anthropic is also launching a free AI-powered vulnerability scanning service for open-source software projects, called OSS Scanner.

  • Participating projects will receive periodic scans from Claude, along with automated reports detailing vulnerabilities, how they could be exploited and suggested fixes.
  • The reports won't undergo human review before being sent to software maintainers, meaning some findings could be inaccurate.

The big picture: Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI developers are looking for ways to put their most powerful models in the hands of cyber defenders as hackers gain access to similar capabilities.

  • Anthropic's new initiative builds on lessons from Project Glasswing, which gave vetted organizations access to its most capable AI models to identify security vulnerabilities.
  • The company said the project demonstrated how quickly AI can uncover vulnerabilities, but also how difficult it remains to verify and fix them.

Yes, but: It's unclear how participating companies will safely test and deploy fixes without disrupting utilities' operations, one of the biggest challenges in securing critical infrastructure.

  • Anthropic also didn't specify whether partners will receive free model access or who will cover the computing costs associated with using its AI tools.

Go deeper: AI is supercharging hacks of everyday utilities

item.title: Trump: Anyone saying "AI" is "THE ENEMY!" The White House uses it
item.description:
President Trump on Thursday called anyone who uses "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" "THE ENEMY!" — even as the White House continues using the term "AI."

Why it matters: Trump's push to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" clashes with established terminology in the technology industry.

  • Trump's branding blurs the distinction between AI and super intelligence, a hypothetical version of AI more advanced than human intelligence.

What they're saying: "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday.

Zoom out: Trump's executive order from September doubled down on using "SI" over "AI," though it did not offer a penalty for using the term.

  • The order specifically defines "Super Intelligence" using the existing federal legal definition of AI.
  • The order calls on federal agencies to change how they describe AI in official communications.
  • The State Department already ordered diplomats to use the term after Trump's United Nations speech on Sept. 22.

Yes, but: The White House still uses "AI" as a term, including on the Office of Science and Technology Policy website, which makes reference to "artificial intelligence."

  • On Thursday, the White House updated its AI.gov website to read "SI.gov" in a massive font. The URL is still "AI.gov," though, with "SI.gov" leading to an error page.
  • When an Axios reporter asked the America.gov chatbot about AI, the bot responded: "The executive branch uses Super Intelligence (SI) for this topic, not the older term you used."

What we're watching: Whether the White House could update its websites to reflect Trump's preferred terminology.

  • The White House did not respond to Axios' request for comment Thursday.

Editor's note: This article has been updated to reflect the White House's change of its AI.gov website to read "SI.gov."

item.title: Trump's foreign worker crackdown comes for Microsoft, Adobe, IT firms
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the Trump administration is suspending Microsoft, Adobe and several other IT firms' ability to hire foreign-born workers for permanent residency in the U.S.

Why it matters: The move will affect hundreds of companies owned by the tech giant, escalating the Trump administration's crackdown on immigrant labor.

What they're saying: "We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector," Vance said during a Thursday news conference.

  • "We're the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers."
  • "And so our message to Microsoft is, you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants."

Zoom in: The permanent labor certification program, which is administered through the Department of Labor, allows a company to hire foreign workers to live permanently in America.

  • It's typically the first step in receiving an employer-sponsored green card. It's also separate from H-1B visas, which allow workers to live and work temporarily in the U.S.
  • H-1B visas primarily go to highly skilled workers in specialized occupations. Technology companies are among the program's biggest users.
  • The Trump administration has made reducing the number of foreign workers in the country a rallying cry, and accused foreign-born workers of taking jobs that could — and, in its view, should — go to Americans.

Driving the news: Vance specifically singled out Microsoft, slamming them for laying off 6,000 workers last year.

  • Vance said Thursday that "[a]t the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. Now that is a scandalous system that we've allowed in this country for far too long."
  • Microsoft owns hundreds of companies, including LinkedIn, Skype and gaming studio Activision Blizzard.
  • Adobe and IT outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini are also suspended from the program.

The other side: "We believe in the strength and talent of the American workforce," Microsoft said in a statement.

  • "That is why the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans. We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information."
  • "For example, of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country."
  • Microsoft also said it only files H-1B petitions for people who "meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and that they pay H-1B workers comparable compensation to other employees."

Worth noting: Trump will award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House today.

  • Microsoft did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the Trump administration is suspending Microsoft, Adobe and several other IT firms' ability to hire foreign-born workers for permanent residency in the U.S.

Why it matters: The move will affect hundreds of companies owned by the tech giant, escalating the Trump administration's crackdown on immigrant labor.

What they're saying: "We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector," Vance said during a Thursday news conference.

  • "We're the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers."
  • "And so our message to Microsoft is, you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants."

Zoom in: The permanent labor certification program, which is administered through the Department of Labor, allows a company to hire foreign workers to live permanently in America.

  • It's typically the first step in receiving an employer-sponsored green card. It's also separate from H-1B visas, which allow workers to live and work temporarily in the U.S.
  • H-1B visas primarily go to highly skilled workers in specialized occupations. Technology companies are among the program's biggest users.
  • The Trump administration has made reducing the number of foreign workers in the country a rallying cry, and accused foreign-born workers of taking jobs that could — and, in its view, should — go to Americans.

item.title: Trump: U.S. won't attack Iran before midterms
item.description:
President Trump said Thursday the U.S. will not attack Iran ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Why it matters: Trump had been considering for several days resuming major combat operations before the midterms. However, his past statements about his intentions in Iran haven't always matched what he ultimately did.

  • If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include large-scale strikes on Iranian energy facilities, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say.
  • Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterms, in part because oil prices might rise in response. It could also influence Israel's elections, which are scheduled for Oct. 27.

What he's saying: "I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait ... we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Flashback: In June 2025, before Operation Midnight Hammer, the White House said Trump would decide "within two weeks" whether the U.S. would join Israel's war against Iran. When he made that statement, he had already decided to attack Iran's nuclear sites.

  • On Feb. 27, less than 24 hours before Israel and the U.S. launched the war against Iran, Trump claimed he hadn't made a decision on going to war. In reality, Trump had already decided to authorize the attacks.

Driving the news: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran, Axios reported on Wednesday.

Behind the scenes: On Tuesday, Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke with senior U.S. officials who briefed him on the U.S. military's preparations for the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a U.S. official and another source briefed on the call.

  • Zamir said during the call that resuming the war within that timeframe could lead to the postponement of the Israeli elections, given the assessment that Iran would respond by launching missiles at Israel, the sources said.
  • The IDF declined to comment on conversations between Zamir and his U.S. counterparts.

Between the lines: It's unclear whether Trump's statement will reassure Iranian leaders that an attack is not imminent.

  • U.S. and Israeli officials say Iranian leaders are deeply suspicious of Trump's statements.
  • The officials said Iranian leaders were surprised twice and want to avoid a third surprise attack.

What to watch: Trump said the U.S. and Iran "are having productive discussions." But there are no signs that the major differences between the two sides have narrowed.

item.title: Labor Department marks low layoffs milestone
item.description:
Data: U.S. Department of Labor; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

New applications for unemployment benefits have stayed below 200,000 in a stretch rarely seen in modern history.

  • Jobless claims fell by 2,000, to 197,000, last week, the Labor Department said Thursday morning.

Why it matters: It points to a remarkable stability on the "firing" side of the labor market, even amid a slower pace of hiring on the other side of the equation.

  • That is helping to keep unemployment low, but it also masks a growing divide between Americans who have jobs and those struggling to find one.

What they're saying: "New jobless claims have been under 200,000 for a month now, an incredibly low level of layoffs for a sustained period of time that hasn't been seen since the 1960s," Navy Federal Credit Union chief economist Heather Long said.

By the numbers: The four-week average, which smooths out weekly volatility, fell to 198,000, its lowest level since the red-hot job market of 2022–2023.

The other side: Jobless claims don't capture every layoff. Some workers receive severance, don't qualify for benefits or find the application process too cumbersome.

  • Still, when layoffs have surged across the economy, claims have surged with them — including during the recessions after the financial crisis and the pandemic. The absence of such an increase now is hard to dismiss.
  • Other data tells a similar story: Announced job cuts fell 20% from a year earlier in September, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

The bottom line: Employers may be reluctant to hire, but they appear just as reluctant to fire — an unusual combination that, for now, keeps the labor market on steady footing.

item.title: The Fed's going to take its time with rate hikes
item.description:
A couple more interest rate hikes are probably on the way. But the Federal Reserve is in no great hurry to deliver them. That's the takeaway from the latest round of communications out of the central bank.

Why it matters: It implies that the Fed is not in a full-scale effort to tighten the screws on the economy, but rather a cautious recalibration in light of inflationary pressures and robust growth.

  • With Fed chairman Kevin Warsh declining to offer much in the way of guidance, traders and Fed watchers must look to other communications for clues — and the message has been strikingly consistent across the latest crumbs of information.

Driving the news: Speaking Thursday morning in Istanbul, Fed governor Christopher Waller explained, with distinctly non-Warshian detail, what kind of interest rate path he anticipates.

  • "If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal," he said.
  • "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
  • That aligns with the language in the minutes of the September policy meeting released Wednesday afternoon, stating that "most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year-end," but that they "approached each meeting with an open mind."

Of note: The minutes and Waller comments come after fairly explicit comments last week from vice chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams waving away expectations of a second rate increase at a meeting concluding Oct. 28.

Zoom in: That doesn't answer the question of how big this tightening cycle will turn out to be. But the tea leaves point to one more rate hike at this year's final meeting and another early in 2027.

  • That would amount to a total of 0.75 percentage point of rate increases, the same size adjustment as easing cycles in 2019 and 2025.
  • Waller, in an extended musing about Fed communication strategy in Thursday morning's speech, used a 0.75-point adjustment as the hypothetical cumulative adjustment. If nothing else, it's a hint that he sees three rate hikes in this adjustment cycle as the most probable course of action.

Between the lines: Warsh is determined to maintain optionality and not pre-commit to a policy path, and he still has that. But talk of leaving rates steady in October and keeping the cumulative adjustment modest tells us something about what kind of rate cycle Fed leadership envisions.

  • This is not — in their view, at least — the beginning of a sustained, open-ended tightening cycle needed to slow the economy and break the back of inflation, as last seen in 2022.
  • Rather, it's a take-your-time, limited operation to better calibrate policy for the mix of solid labor market results, accelerating growth and elevated inflation that they see.

What they're saying: "With evidence that economic activity is strengthening in the second half of this year, I am not greatly concerned that tighter monetary policy threatens a damaging slowdown in the economy," Waller said Thursday morning.

  • "But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation."

The bottom line: Investors can take solace that the Fed is not preparing aggressive action to take away the punchbowl. The open question is whether this limited tightening will do the trick in getting inflation down faster.

item.title: Nicolás Maduro and his wife hit with fresh torture charge
item.description:
Prosecutors accused former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife of orchestrating the torture of people held in his regime's custody, piling onto the narcoterrorism charges they already face in a fresh indictment unveiled Thursday.

The big picture: The charges add new fuel to the historic prosecution seeking to hold the strongman-turned-prisoner accountable for alleged crimes against Americans and alleged abuse of power.

  • Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, pleaded not guilty in January to drug- and weapon-related charges. They have been held in the U.S. since their stunning capture from Caracas earlier this year.
  • Maduro's attorney did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Driving the news: Maduro "authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention, and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," a superseding indictment filed in the Southern District of New York alleged.

  • The new indictment charges Maduro and Flores with conspiracy to commit torture, alleging they engaged in a conspiracy to inflict "severe physical and mental pain and suffering to repress and punish political opposition."

What's inside: The indictment outlines a series of disturbing torture tactics — including electrocution, beatings, isolation and simulated drowning — allegedly employed at Maduro's direction to quell political opposition.

  • "As opposition to the ruling regime intensified," Maduro allegedly "continued to oversee the development of a more systematic approach to unlawfully arresting and torturing dissidents," per the indictment, ordering who would be arrested and tortured.
  • One unnamed victim who the indictment described as "friendly" with "a famous opponent of the regime" was told by his captors that they would kill his young child, whose hair color they referenced.
  • It also details abuse against Americans, including one who was allegedly falsely accused of participating in a conspiracy to kill Maduro. That victim was allegedly tortured with electric shocks, asphyxiation and forced injection of a substance that made him have seizures.

Catch up quick: Americans who were formerly imprisoned in Venezuela have accused Maduro of heading a web of corruption that used Americans as negotiating tools.

  • In a lawsuit filed last year, Matthew Heath and Osman Khan, two Americans freed in a 2022 prisoner swap, alleged they were subjected to electrocution, suffocation, severe beatings and food and water deprivation, among other threats and forms of torture.
  • Members of a group of oil executives, known as the CITGO-6, also released in October 2022, alleged they faced physical and emotional torture while in Venezuelan custody.

What's next: Their trial is set to begin on June 1, 2027.

  • Flores' legal team has sought her release ahead of the trial, citing her heart issues and saying that since she's entered custody, she's lost two molars and more than 25 pounds.

Go deeper: Maduro ally pleads guilty to money laundering

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: DNC sues to stop Trump's taxpayer-funded ad blitz
item.description:
President Trump said he will help pay for his administration's campaign-style ads after the Democratic National Committee sued Wednesday over their use of taxpayer money.

Why it matters: Trump's funding announcement does not address the DNC's central allegation that the administration illegally used taxpayer money to finance the ads.

What they're saying: Trump said in a Truth Social post that he considers the ads "to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A." and defended using taxpayer money for them.

  • "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself," Trump wrote.
  • Trump said money from MAGA Inc., his superPAC, would also pay for the ads.
  • A person familiar with the advertising plans said the existing taxpayer-funded ad buy will end this week, after which outside groups will begin paying for the spots.

The White House defended the ads as public service announcements, arguing that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies.

  • The White House said the ads are not political because Trump is not on the ballot and the spots contain no call to action.

The other side: "These ads are a clear violation of the Congressional ban on the use of appropriated funds for 'publicity or propaganda purposes,'" the DNC's legal counsel wrote in the lawsuit.

  • "The president has nationalized the midterm election, made himself the center of a two-day 'midterm convention,' and repeatedly directed voters to 'pretend that I am on the ballot," it added.
  • "As the 2026 midterm election has approached, Republican poll numbers have plummeted in both traditional battlegrounds and typically favorable states, and Democrats are poised to take control of Congress, governors' mansions, and state legislatures around the country."

Zoom in: The lawsuit alleges the White House crafted the ads to boost the president's approval ratings and help Republican candidates.

  • The complaint largely focuses on its allegation that the ads were paid for with money originally allocated for Customs and Border Protection that was rerouted for the TV spots.
  • The DNC argues that the ads violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the Antideficiency Act, and the Purpose Act.

Zoom out: The administration was also hit with a second lawsuit over the ads Wednesday from pro-democracy group Common Cause, a state legislative candidate, a service union and an affiliated PAC.

  • "[W]ithout this Court's intervention," the similar suit alleges, "Defendants will continue to run nakedly partisan ads that admit they are "Paid for by the U.S. Government" to Plaintiffs' detriment."

The DNC asked a federal judge to step in, declare the administration's actions illegal and immediately block them from airing any more ads paid for with taxpayer money.

  • It's not clear how the judge will rule, given President Trump said Monday that a Trump-affiliated super PAC would begin paying for the ads moving forward.
  • A White House spokesperson confirmed Tuesday to Axios that the administration would not repay the government for the ads.

Catch up quick: According to the suit, Trump personally hand-picked the ads that aired on television, which were broadcast to millions of Americans, including during NFL and college football games.

  • The lawsuit says the ads aired "nearly 90 times across national television networks, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now, and CBS" over four days in late September. Those spots likely cost around $337,000.
  • In that same time period, the ads aired on local television stations at least 2,311 times and those placements cost around $1.4 million, the suit says.
  • Advertisement tracking firm AdImpact estimates that over $2.5 million was spent on the ads the first week they were aired.

Worth noting: Using public funds for campaign ads hasn't sat well with American voters.

  • Nearly nine in ten voters said in a Reuters-Ipsos poll published Wednesday that using taxpayer money for campaign ads featuring a president or Cabinet member is inappropriate.

Go deeper: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up

Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

  • "[W]ithout this Court's intervention," the similar suit alleges, "Defendants will continue to run nakedly partisan ads that admit they are "Paid for by the U.S. Government" to Plaintiffs' detriment."

The DNC asked a federal judge to step in, declare the administration's actions illegal and immediately block them from airing any more ads paid for with taxpayer money.

  • It's not clear how the judge will rule, given President Trump said Monday that a Trump-affiliated super PAC would begin paying for the ads moving forward.
  • A White House spokesperson confirmed Tuesday to Axios that the administration would not repay the government for the ads.

Catch up quick: According to the suit, Trump personally hand-picked the ads that aired on television, which were broadcast to millions of Americans, including during NFL and college football games.

  • The lawsuit says the ads aired "nearly 90 times across national television networks, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now, and CBS" over four days in late September. Those spots likely cost around $337,000.
  • In that same time period, the ads aired on local television stations at least 2,311 times and those placements cost around $1.4 million, the suit says.
  • Advertisement tracking firm AdImpact estimates that over $2.5 million was spent on the ads the first week they were aired.

Worth noting: Using public funds for campaign ads hasn't sat well with American voters.

  • Nearly nine in ten voters said in a Reuters-Ipsos poll published Wednesday that using taxpayer money for campaign ads featuring a president or Cabinet member is inappropriate.

Go deeper: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up

Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

item.title: Republicans squirm as Latino support slips in South Texas
item.description:
Republicans are in a dogfight to defend the Latino gains that had them dreaming of a lasting political realignment just two years ago.

Why it matters: Nowhere is that reversal of fortune more visible than in South Texas, where President Trump ran up historic numbers in 2024 — and Republicans redrew the map in 2025, assuming those Latino gains would last.

  • Trump won 55% of Texas Latino voters in 2024 exit polls, carried 14 of the 18 counties within 20 miles of the border and won all four Rio Grande Valley counties.
  • Polling shows Trump's disapproval ratings have skyrocketed among Latinos in Texas since 2024.
  • Democrats and allied groups are now pouring money into races across the Rio Grande Valley.

Zoom in: The reversal is starkest in TX-15, where Rep. Monica De La Cruz was one of the GOP's most visible symbols of its South Texas breakthrough.

  • Trump would have carried the newly-drawn district by 18 percentage points in 2024. De La Cruz won her 2024 race under the previous map by 14 points.
  • Cook Political Report moved the race from Lean Republican to Toss Up on Sept. 25, saying public and private polling shows the race tied or even favoring Tejano singer and Democrat Bobby Pulido.

By the numbers: Democratic campaigns and allied groups are outspending Republican campaigns and groups on Spanish-language ads in two of the three competitive House districts covering the Rio Grande Valley, according to AdImpact data reported by the Texas Tribune.

  • In TX-34, held by Vicente Gonzalez (D), Democratic campaigns and groups have spent $2.7 million on Spanish-language ads, compared with $1.6 million on the Republican side.
  • In TX-15, Democratic groups have spent more than twice as much as Republican groups on Spanish-language ads.
  • TX-28 bucks the trend: Republicans have narrowly outspent Democrats on Spanish-language ads to unseat Henry Cuellar (D).

Zoom out: TX-34 is also a Toss Up, while TX-28 is Lean Democratic.

  • The newly redrawn TX-35 has moved from Likely Republican to Lean Republican.
  • House Majority PAC launched another round of ads Tuesday in TX-15, TX-28 and TX-34, defending two Democratic incumbents while continuing to target De La Cruz.

The bottom line: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll shows Latinos nationally favor Democratic control of Congress 59%-35%, a 24-point advantage — roughly double the margin the same poll found for Democrats in 2024.

  • A recent TelevisaUnivision poll found Latino voters in the three competitive Texas House districts shifting from a 44%-44% split in their 2024 presidential vote to 56%-36% Democratic on the 2026 congressional ballot.

item.title: "The Axios Show": Inside Bryan Johnson's quest to make 300 the new 70
item.description:
Bryan Johnson, the face of the longevity movement, wants to make staying alive more important than making money.

  • The famous/infamous biohacker spends over $2 million a year on his health, talks about living forever and publicly tracks everything from his erections to his sperm strength.

Why it matters: As Johnson fights to "live forever," he's doing so with a wink to his 8 million social media followers, a link to his business in his bio and a knack for drawing attention to himself.

What they're saying: In his interview with The Axios Show, he offered some advice for Elon Musk, said he'd love to help President Trump with his health and revealed his ultimate goal.

  • "Will the 25th century ... be like, 'thank you' in 500 years? Will they give me a head nod? That's the goal," he said.

Zoom out: His big picture focus: change the focus of society to health, not wealth.

  • "Society says making money... is the greatest trophy one can get...we are at this inflection moment as a species where we are transitioning to 'Don't Die,'" Johnson said, referring to the title of his longevity movement.
  • "What creates status and power and prestige is going to be different. And as crazy as it sounds, it may be your nighttime erections...It may be your ability to dunk a basketball at age 49," he said.
  • Johnson, 49, is currently trying to dunk.

Zoom out: That focus is what drives some of his more extreme experiments and interventions.

  • In 2023, Johnson injected his teenage son's plasma, which he found to be a helpful regimen for his dad but not for himself, saying his own biomarkers are already "pretty similar to my 18-year-old."
  • Through the help of wearables, tests and a concierge team, Johnson has gathered over 4.2 billion data points about his own body and health, and he relies on AI tools to help parse takeaways from that data.
  • He has an in-home medical lab of sorts where he can do continuous testing, monitoring and procedures.

Zoom in: Perhaps his most extreme act is his online presence, which Johnson called "performance art" in our conversation.

  • When talking about humans dramatically increasing lifespans through scientific methods, "no one cares," he said. But "if you talk about it in performance art where it has a vibe and an energy to it, people will engage."

The intrigue: Still, even Johnson recommends many of the basics for health: sleep, healthy diet and exercise.

  • For those who want to go further, he recommends a blood draw or MRI, sitting in a sauna several times a week and testing out psychedelics.
  • When asked which longevity treatments feel like snake oil, Johnson said "Basically everything on social media."
  • When I pointed out that includes Bryan, he said, "you're right. I've done this for years. Most things don't work."

Reality check: Johnson has multiple longevity businesses that he calls successful, though the financials of the companies are not public.

  • Blueprint, his consumer products business, sells "the most tested healthy longevity protocols," per the company: protein powders, supplements and even extra virgin olive oil.
  • Immortals, another one of his companies, offers concierge longevity care for a limited group of members. Prices range from $75,000 a year to $1 million per year.
  • Johnson has "very complicated emotions about this business because I started the company to try to help other people and not to make money. ...I'd rather just be clean and be like, "I'm going to help you out." But to help people out, I have to have infrastructure to actually deliver these things."

The intrigue: Johnson said he gets calls from world leaders asking for his advice, and he's in group chats with top tech leaders and influencers.

  • When asked for his health advice for Elon Musk, Johnson said "I hope Elon would clean up his health. I mean, he's worked so hard. He has a lot of potential to enjoy what he's built."

The bottom line: Johnson believes wealth is out, health and longevity are in as the new status symbols.

item.title: Inside Trump's blow-up at Fox News over El-Sayed coverage
item.description:
Republicans have spent months griping privately to Fox News about coverage they argue is helping Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's Democratic nominee for Senate, moderate his image. The frustration boiled into public view Tuesday when President Trump lashed out at his favorite network.

Why it matters: Republicans worry that Fox is undercutting their efforts to brand the charismatic El-Sayed as a liberal who's far outside the mainstream.

  • Polls show El-Sayed, a critic of Israel's government who'd be the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, in a tight race against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R).

Behind the scenes: White House officials reached out to Fox on Tuesday to complain about anchor Martha MacCallum's interview with El-Sayed, according to people familiar with the conversations. On Truth Social, Trump blasted the interview as "softball."

  • "Fox is promoting the Dumocrats, not the Republicans and MAGA. They have totally lost their way!" he wrote.

The White House's frustration over Fox's coverage of El-Sayed had been bubbling for weeks before Trump's post.

  • Senior GOP operatives repeatedly contacted Fox producers and executives in early August, warning that El-Sayed could use favorable commentary from host Jesse Watters to cast himself as moderate.
  • After El-Sayed's upset primary win over an establishment-backed candidate, Watters said: "You gotta respect Abdul because he beat the [Democratic] machine."

Later that month, El-Sayed released a TV ad featuring Watters' remark. His campaign called Watters an "unlikely validator."

  • Republicans were reassured when Watters pressed El-Sayed on his criticism of ICE, support for Medicare for All and opinion on Sharia law during an Aug. 24 interview — only to be frustrated again when Watters said the next day: "I actually like Abdul. I probably shouldn't like him, but I do."

State of play: Fox News has become a significant part of El-Sayed's effort to reach voters beyond the Democratic base.

  • From Oct. 1 to 6, El-Sayed campaign ads aired 129 times on Fox News — roughly twice as often as they did on ESPN, according to ad-tracking data.
  • Michigan-based GOP strategist Dennis Lennox told Axios: "It's not just that he is doing interviews with Fox. It's that he is on Fox every commercial break."

Between the lines: Republicans acknowledge El-Sayed has shown he can hold his own under tough questioning — even when pressed on issues the GOP is using against him.

  • El-Sayed said during Monday's interview with MacCallum: "I am going to have conversations with all kinds of folks."

According to Fox, Watters' interview with El-Sayed in August drew nearly 3.4 million viewers, making it the highest-rated cable news primetime telecast of the month.

  • Michigan-based GOP strategist Jason Roe told Axios: "They are doing him a favor. It's only helping him reach center-right voters. But they are in business to make money, and he attracts eyeballs."

The other side: A Fox News spokesperson said Rogers also was invited to be interviewed on Watters' show but didn't respond.

  • White House officials noted in their conversation with Fox that El-Sayed had recently turned down a private offer from Rogers to debate on the network, according to a source with knowledge of the talks.

Jay Wallace, Fox News Media president and executive editor, told Axios on Tuesday that MacCallum's interview of El-Sayed reflected the network's willingness to air programming its core audience may not want to hear.

  • "Someone didn't necessarily like that," Wallace said, apparently referring to Trump. "But that's what we do."

item.title: OpenAI's math breakthrough points beyond math
item.description:
AI's conquest of computer programming offered an early demonstration of what happens when models become good enough at a specialized field that experts can no longer treat them as a novelty.

  • Mathematics appears to be next.

Why it matters: OpenAI's latest mathematical results — which involved releasing hundreds of new proofs generated by a powerful, unreleased model — demonstrate that the startling advances of AI are likely to continue moving across entirely new fields.

Catch up quick: OpenAI on Tuesday released 722 manuscripts organized into 372 groups of findings ("families") on long-standing mathematical problems, inviting academics and researchers to examine and build on the material.

  • The reception has mixed scientific excitement with genuine unease. One Rutgers University mathematician said on X that a result connected to the Riemann hypothesis would warrant an automatic Fields Medal if a human had done the work.
  • Some mathematicians have questioned these results, as well as another solution OpenAI released last month, asking whether they represent original breakthroughs or draw heavily from previous human input.
  • Others downplayed the utility of AI-generated math. "You can discover new math easily," Stephen Wolfram, a renowned computer scientist and physicist who has followed AI closely for years, said at a Tuesday event for the National Museum of Mathematics. "You can make a trillion theorems easily. The problem is most of those theorems are not ones that anybody will care about."

Zoom in: Like computer programming, mathematics gives AI something unusually valuable: a way to tell when it is right.

  • A proof can be scrutinized by mathematicians and, increasingly, translated into formal languages that computers can verify line by line. Similarly, it is immediately possible to know whether autonomously written AI code actually works.

The big picture: Software engineers have already lived through this transition.

  • AI coding tools progressed from autocomplete and debugging to agents capable of writing substantial amounts of software and carrying out complex engineering tasks.
  • The shift has changed not only how code gets written, but what it means to be a programmer, bringing a fair dose of awe, amazement and dread to many lifelong software engineers.
  • Much as software engineers did before them, mathematicians have begun to question the implications of some of the OpenAI discoveries on graduate work, and on training a new generation of theorists.

Yes, but: Some software engineers have successfully mapped out the roles humans still play in generating quality products. While new AI coding tools have dramatically increased the code one engineer can ship, humans still play a crucial role in building quality software.

  • Mathematicians have begun to echo that point, noting that the most meaningful advances in their field often involve building a framework or bringing structure to a complex idea. Many are skeptical about whether any AI system will be able to replicate human originality.

Between the lines: Beyond mathematics, the results do point to the likelihood that AI disruption will continue moving into new areas, partially answering a long-standing question from AI skeptics.

  • While researchers at rival startups questioned the utility of OpenAI's mathematical findings because of limited practical applications, some acknowledged that they provide evidence of AI's rapid advances.

item.title: Data centers face a sweeping new power regime
item.description:
Lawmakers are considering forcing data centers to shoulder new costs and restrictions while speeding up the energy infrastructure needed to power the AI boom.

Why it matters: The bipartisan legislation, unveiled last week, represents the most aggressive response yet from Washington to data centers amid growing backlash over their energy and environmental impacts.

Driving the news: The provisions are part of broader Senate legislation aimed at speeding up permitting for energy — but make no mistake: The data center measures are significant and would go far beyond Washington's largely voluntary efforts to date.

  • The bill's sponsors say it would accelerate energy development while ensuring data centers pay their share of grid upgrades.

"I don't think we've seen it before," said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, about the proposed additional costs and restrictions.

  • "But I don't think we've seen growth that's comparable to data centers today, and I certainly don't know any industry whose electricity usage has captured so much political attention."

Between the lines: For tech companies, the bill cuts both ways. Congress would make it easier to build the energy infrastructure they need while erecting a sweeping framework aimed at keeping other electricity customers from footing the bill.

"Just to be candid, having some teeth on data center accountability and ratepayer protection is just table stakes to getting a deal done," said Jane Flegal, a former White House official under President Biden and now a senior fellow at the nonprofit Searchlight Institute.

The big picture: Congress has been talking about overhauling permitting for years. The AI boom has given lawmakers an urgent reason to finally act: America suddenly needs enormous amounts of new power infrastructure, fast.

  • Faster approvals for power plants and transmission lines could directly benefit data centers struggling to secure enough electricity for their expansion.

How it works: The bill reaches into virtually every part of the relationship between large data centers and the electric grid.

  • Data centers would be required to pay both their share of the existing transmission network and the incremental transmission costs needed to serve them, reversing a decades-old federal pricing policy that generally prevents charging both. This is the biggie, but it doesn't stop there.
  • New data centers of at least 20 megawatts would have to bear the incremental costs they impose across the power system, including generation, storage, transmission and distribution.
  • Regulators at both the federal and state levels could charge large data centers even more than those incremental costs — and use the excess to reduce other customers' bills.
  • Data centers would remain on the hook for infrastructure costs even if they stop buying electricity before those costs have been recovered. Utilities would also have to secure financial guarantees before building infrastructure to serve them, protecting ratepayers if projects don't materialize.

Zoom in: States are already moving aggressively to protect ratepayers, with dozens of policies pending or in place across more than half the states aimed at making data centers shoulder more of the costs of serving them.

  • The bill would explicitly give states wide latitude to go further, including treating data centers less favorably than other large industrial customers, competitively allocating access to electricity and requiring them to secure new power supplies or accept limits on electricity use.

What they're saying: Not much publicly, yet. The Data Center Coalition, which represents companies across the industry, said it is still reviewing the legislation.

  • Microsoft, Google and Nvidia declined to comment, while Meta didn't respond to a request for comment.
  • Amazon energy policy director Craig Sundstrom said the aging grid and slow permitting are putting pressure on electricity costs, adding that the bill "could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster."

The intrigue: One tech industry official called some provisions an "unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment" for a single industry.

  • The official, who spoke anonymously to discuss industry deliberations, said tougher grid-connected requirements could encourage some developers to build more power systems completely off-grid instead — potentially undermining the overarching purpose of the bill.

The other side: Travis Fisher, a former Trump White House energy official now at the libertarian Cato Institute, said he has "mild support" for the approach despite concerns about setting a discriminatory precedent.

  • He said the provisions "break new ground" at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission but are consistent with the White House's ratepayer-protection pledge many of the largest data center companies have already signed.

What we're watching: Flegal said she would be "incredibly surprised" if tech companies ultimately oppose the broader package.

What's next: With the Senate out of town ahead of the midterm elections, lawmakers and stakeholders have plenty of time to push for changes before a possible lame-duck debate.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

  • "But I don't think we've seen growth that's comparable to data centers today, and I certainly don't know any industry whose electricity usage has captured so much political attention."

Between the lines: For tech companies, the bill cuts both ways. Congress would make it easier to build the energy infrastructure they need while erecting a sweeping framework aimed at keeping other electricity customers from footing the bill.

"Just to be candid, having some teeth on data center accountability and ratepayer protection is just table stakes to getting a deal done," said Jane Flegal, a former White House official under President Biden and now a senior fellow at the nonprofit Searchlight Institute.

The big picture: Congress has been talking about overhauling permitting for years. The AI boom has given lawmakers an urgent reason to finally act: America suddenly needs enormous amounts of new power infrastructure, fast.

  • Faster approvals for power plants and transmission lines could directly benefit data centers struggling to secure enough electricity for their expansion.

How it works: The bill reaches into virtually every part of the relationship between large data centers and the electric grid.

  • Data centers would be required to pay both their share of the existing transmission network and the incremental transmission costs needed to serve them, reversing a decades-old federal pricing policy that generally prevents charging both. This is the biggie, but it doesn't stop there.
  • New data centers of at least 20 megawatts would have to bear the incremental costs they impose across the power system, including generation, storage, transmission and distribution.
  • Regulators at both the federal and state levels could charge large data centers even more than those incremental costs — and use the excess to reduce other customers' bills.
  • Data centers would remain on the hook for infrastructure costs even if they stop buying electricity before those costs have been recovered. Utilities would also have to secure financial guarantees before building infrastructure to serve them, protecting ratepayers if projects don't materialize.

Zoom in: States are already moving aggressively to protect ratepayers, with dozens of policies pending or in place across more than half the states aimed at making data centers shoulder more of the costs of serving them.

  • The bill would explicitly give states wide latitude to go further, including treating data centers less favorably than other large industrial customers, competitively allocating access to electricity and requiring them to secure new power supplies or accept limits on electricity use.

What they're saying: Not much publicly, yet. The Data Center Coalition, which represents companies across the industry, said it is still reviewing the legislation.

  • Microsoft, Google and Nvidia declined to comment, while Meta didn't respond to a request for comment.
  • Amazon energy policy director Craig Sundstrom said the aging grid and slow permitting are putting pressure on electricity costs, adding that the bill "could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster."

The intrigue: One tech industry official called some provisions an "unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment" for a single industry.

  • The official, who spoke anonymously to discuss industry deliberations, said tougher grid-connected requirements could encourage some developers to build more power systems completely off-grid instead — potentially undermining the overarching purpose of the bill.

The other side: Travis Fisher, a former Trump White House energy official now at the libertarian Cato Institute, said he has "mild support" for the approach despite concerns about setting a discriminatory precedent.

  • He said the provisions "break new ground" at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission but are consistent with the White House's ratepayer-protection pledge many of the largest data center companies have already signed.

What we're watching: Flegal said she would be "incredibly surprised" if tech companies ultimately oppose the broader package.

What's next: With the Senate out of town ahead of the midterm elections, lawmakers and stakeholders have plenty of time to push for changes before a possible lame-duck debate.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Republican midterm triage puts bleak outlook into focus
item.description:
Republican super PACs are flooding the airwaves in once-safe states, and pulling down ads for races that look like lost causes. President Trump, his approval ratings near record lows, is popping up in some of America's reddest states.

Why it matters: The polls showing Democrats headed toward a blue wave on Nov. 3 may not be quite right. But money — and how campaigns and PACs spend it — rarely lies. Nor do the contrails of Air Force One.

  • While Republicans are scrambling, Democrats are cutting some spending in contests they think are in the bag, such as North Carolina's Senate race.
  • No one wants to pay too much for a landslide, just as no one wants to throw good money after bad.

Republicans have been forced to pour well over $100 million into Ken Paxton's Senate race in Texas against Democrat James Talarico, and to plead for millions more to defend Senate seats in Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

  • Call it political triage. Republican operatives are making the kind of hard decisions that would be familiar to any battlefield medic: Save the wounded, and say a prayer for the lost.

Driving the news: Trump was in San Antonio on Wednesday to try to boost Paxton — his second trip in less than a week to Texas, a state he won by 14 points in 2024.

  • During the past week the president also has campaigned in Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska. He's planning another trip to Alabama this weekend for the Georgia-Alabama football game.
  • Vice President Vance showed up in Alaska this week, and will be in Ohio this weekend.

What they're saying: Republicans' efforts now appear more focused on calling for party loyalists to show up at the polls than on persuading new voters.

  • "Every time they up a buy [ads] on their end, it's always in the red states," said J.B. Poersch, president of Senate Majority PAC, the Democrats' main outside group working to win the Senate.
  • "Some of these outside [GOP] groups such as the Senate Leadership Fund and others are going to have to figure out where their money is best spent," said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost the GOP primary to Paxton.
  • "It looks like the money has already started to shift."

Zoom in: After pulling out of North Carolina (which Trump won by 3 points) last Friday, the SLF — Republicans' main Senate super PAC — put a fresh $14 million in normally deep-red Kansas.

  • This week, it sent a $5 million "insurance policy" to South Carolina (which Trump won by 18 points) to boost Republican Sen. Darline Graham.

The other side: Democrats are pulling down some advertising, but in states where polling has solidified in their favor. Their spending moves reflect confidence, not concern.

  • After the Senate Republicans' PAC cried uncle and pulled out of North Carolina, the Senate Democrats' group decided to go dark there as well.
  • One of Democratic group's ad reservations for North Carolina — which was actually in the Greenville market in South Carolina — was gobbled up by an allied group, Fresh Start SC PAC, which will use the time to attack Graham.

Between the lines: There's triage campaigning in House races as well, but it's not as pronounced — yet.

  • The GOP's Congressional Leadership Fund pulled down $1.1 million in advertising in Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, one of three GOP-held seats where former Vice President Harris won in 2024.
  • Democrats followed suit, with House Majority PAC canceling the $1.1 million it had reserved for the race. Both sides appear to agree that there's no obvious path for Republican Brinker Harding to win the seat left open by retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon.
  • In a San Diego-area House district, the Democratic group pulled down $200,000 in ads in a redistricted seat Harris would have won.

Zoom out: Republicans insist that their reallocation of funds doesn't mean they're admitting that the House or the Senate are lost.

  • One thing neither side disputes: The Senate Leadership Fund, which is closely associated with Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), is well capitalized.
  • That allows it to shore up candidates in red states, which wouldn't be necessary in a better political environment. In Texas, one of its subsidiaries spent $131 million in 17 days — more than $7.7 million a day.
  • The group has announced another $4 million for the Alaska race, bringing its total there to $21 million for Sen. Dan Sullivan, who's being challenged by former Rep. Mary Peltola.
  • In Maine, it has reserved another $8 million, for a total of $50 million for Sen. Susan Collins, who's in a battle with Democrat Troy Jackson.
  • In Michigan, it's putting in another $2 million, for a total of $53 million for former Rep. Mike Rogers in his race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
  • And in Ohio, it's spending another $14 million, bringing the total to $93 million for Sen. John Husted, who faces former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D).

What we're watching: All eyes are on Georgia. SLF announced an initial investment of $44 million there to back Republican Mike Collins, but Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has a healthy lead.

The bottom line: Republicans can dismiss bad polls as noise, or the result of liberal bias.

  • But their concern is evident in their thundering attack ads in red states such as Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

item.title: Exclusive: Mike Johnson raises record $156 million for House GOP
item.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson raised $30 million in the third quarter, bringing his total haul this cycle to $156 million as Republicans fight to hold on to their increasingly endangered majority, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Johnson's team says that's the most raised by a Republican speaker or leader at this point in an election cycle.

  • Johnson has distributed more than $91 million to Republican members, candidates, committees and state parties this cycle, according to figures first shared with Axios.
  • That includes $46 million transferred to the National Republican Congressional Committee, putting him on pace to make the largest cycle transfer to the group by a Republican speaker or leader.
  • He's also sent $21.5 million directly to GOP incumbents and $7 million to challengers.

Zoom out: Johnson's fundraising operation has brought in more than $220 million for House Republicans since he became speaker in October 2023.

  • That's a notable turnaround from when Johnson first took the gavel, when Republicans worried whether the relatively unknown Louisiana Republican could replace former Speaker Kevin McCarthy's formidable fundraising operation.
  • Johnson is also crisscrossing the country to help House Republicans, traveling to more than 40 districts across 22 states in the final stretch before Election Day, Axios previously reported.

What they're saying: "We are focused on getting unprecedented resources to the Districts that will decide the majority," Johnson said in a statement to Axios.

  • "With this continued momentum, we are in place to defy history and defend the House to save America from the far-left!"

State of play: House Republicans have a cash advantage over Democrats.

  • The NRCC ended August with $13 million more in cash on hand than the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, its largest-ever advantage at this point in an election cycle.
  • But the House battlefield has continued to move toward Democrats. Cook Political Report shifted 15 House races toward Democrats last month, while Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 11 races toward Democrats days later.
  • Many of the most competitive races are now in districts President Trump carried in 2024.

item.title: Americans' trust in the food safety net is spoiling
item.description:
Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Americans' confidence in the safety of food on grocery store shelves — and in the federal government's ability to regulate it — has plummeted to new lows according to a new Gallup poll.

The big picture: Simultaneous illness outbreaks put federal regulators under a microscope earlier this year, as layoffs across the nation's health apparatus were already causing food safety angst.

By the numbers: Less than half of U.S. adults have a great deal (11%) or a fair amount (36%) of confidence in the federal government to ensure food safety, according to the poll, which was conducted last month.

  • On the flip side, a majority have not much or no confidence in the government's ability to police their food — a first in Gallup's trend, which has been intermittent for two decades.

Zoom out: Meanwhile, Americans' confidence in the food sold at grocery stores has mirrored that drop, falling to a record low of 65% saying they are somewhat or very confident.

  • That share has plunged from the 81% recorded in 2019.

Zoom in: That growing food safety suspicion is driven by Democrats and independents, while Republicans have actually become more confident in grocery store food.

  • The partisan chasm over the federal government's ability to ensure food safety has flipped — and widened — under the second Trump administration.
  • In 2024, half of Republicans had a great deal or fair amount of confidence in the government to ensure food safety, while nearly three-quarters of Democrats agreed.
  • By 2025, Democrats' confidence fell to 48%, and to 30% in 2026. Republicans, meanwhile, found new faith, with their confidence climbing from 62% in 2025 to 70% to 2026.

Catch up quick: This year's polling occurred during and after the federal government declared the end of an outbreak of Cyclospora, a parasite that caused stomach illnesses, two deaths and saw more than 500 hospitalizations across 21 states.

  • Federal health officials eventually traced the rapidly spreading surge to iceberg lettuce from supplier Taylor Farms.
  • But the food woes didn't stop there: This summer saw a flurry of overlapping recalls and FDA investigations, while health experts warned administration cuts had weakened the public health infrastructure responsible for detecting outbreaks.

Meanwhile, significant shares of Americans report concerns or strain about affording those groceries.

  • The food-at-home CPI, for grocery store or supermarket food purchases, was up 2.2% between August 2025 and 2026.

Friction point: That collides with an administration that's pushed whole foods as part of its "Make America Healthy Again" campaign under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

  • But Gallup's polling indicates Republicans have digested that food safety message far better than Democrats and independents.

Go deeper: America's next grocery shock is brewing

item.title: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
item.description:
The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: The directive didn't include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump hasn't made any final decisions. But U.S. and Israeli sources say it could happen before the U.S. midterm elections and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier.

The big picture: If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say.

  • Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterm elections, in part because oil prices might rise in response.
  • "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told Axios.
  • A White House official said Trump has all options available at any time.
  • "The U.S. is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States."
  • The Atlantic reported earlier Wednesday that Trump is weighing striking Iran before the midterm election.

Driving the news: On Friday, Trump's national security team met at Camp David for several hours to discuss the war and other issues.

  • An Israeli official told Axios that part of the meeting focused on a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that it focused on "long-term" foreign policy planning.
  • Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran haven't made any progress. Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian response to a U.S. counterproposal that included demands for nuclear concessions.
  • "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out. After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly," a second Israeli official said.

Behind the scenes: President Trump spoke Wednesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was their second call in days, after barely speaking for many weeks.

  • A U.S. official said Trump and Netanyahu spoke about "remembrance and respect for the victims of the October 7 massacre."
  • The call took place after Netanyahu held a meeting with his national security team about Iran, the first Israeli official said.
  • Netanyahu spoke to Rubio on Monday.
  • If major combat operations resume, they will most likely be with the U.S. and Israel working in tandem and with the Israeli military participating.
  • The two Israeli officials said the Iranian regime is desperate and paranoid, which might lead it to strike first.
  • They said the Iranians have suffered two surprise attacks and don't want to experience a third.

Between the lines: Resumption of the war could also affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation.

  • A renewed escalation — or even a heightened state of tension or emergency — could benefit Netanyahu politically and prevent his opponents from attacking him in the final stretch of the campaign.

item.title: Student protest unrest spreads across Europe
item.description:
Police and protesters clashed in Liège, Belgium, on Wednesday as student anger over education costs and school conditions grew, echoing massive protests in neighboring France.

Why it matters: The protests are exposing broader anger across Europe over school funding and classroom conditions.

Catch up quick: Protests that began in Paris in mid-September as a localized demonstration by high school students have escalated into a massive nationwide movement, with students, parents and teachers' unions demanding more education funding.

  • There have been clashes between French police and protesters in recent days, culminating in a 15-year-old boy's hand being blown off by a police-fired stun grenade. More than 6,500 people — most of them minors —have been arrested since the protests began in France.
  • In Belgium, police have made at least 139 arrests in Liège since the protests began Oct. 1.

The big picture: The current wave erupted in France, but education grievances across Europe predate it, with crowded classrooms, teacher shortages, university cuts and soaring education costs fueling protests over government investment in education.

In Greece, students called nationwide school actions for Thursday, according to Euronews, including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and potentially occupations.

In Italy, high-school occupations began in Turin and Rome on Monday under the slogan "Let's do as in France."

  • Italian students cited underfunding, deteriorating school buildings and rising living costs among grievances they share with French students, and a delegation traveled to Paris in solidarity, ANSA reports.

In Ireland, thousands of university students demonstrated in Dublin earlier this month, demanding lower fees, more higher-education funding and affordable accommodation, per RTÉ.

In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions rallied in September to demand greater education investment, more teachers and a more equitable school system, according to Tagesschau.

In Austria, student groups are preparing fresh demonstrations in mid-October after the country's university association warned of possible cuts of around €1 billion from the next three-year university budget, ORF reports.

Between the lines: The education unrest comes as several European governments face mounting pressure to rein in deficits while higher borrowing costs make their debts more expensive to service.

  • France and Belgium are each running budget deficits of more than 5% of their GDP this year, while Austria's is above 4%, according to European Commission forecasts.
  • That squeeze is forcing governments to make difficult choices over public spending.

The bottom line: The protests aren't one coordinated European movement, but students across several countries are mobilizing around their shared concerns.

Go deeper: The global fiscal reckoning is here

Catch up quick: Protests that began in Paris in mid-September as a localized demonstration by high school students have escalated into a massive nationwide movement, with students, parents and teachers' unions demanding more education funding.

  • There have been clashes between French police and protesters in recent days, culminating in a 15-year-old boy's hand being blown off by a police-fired stun grenade. More than 6,500 people — most of them minors —have been arrested since the protests began in France.
  • In Belgium, police have made at least 139 arrests in Liège since the protests began Oct. 1.

The big picture: The current wave erupted in France, but education grievances across Europe predate it, with crowded classrooms, teacher shortages, university cuts and soaring education costs fueling protests over government investment in education.

In Greece, students called nationwide school actions for Thursday, according to Euronews, including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and potentially occupations.

In Italy, high-school occupations began in Turin and Rome on Monday under the slogan "Let's do as in France."

  • Italian students cited underfunding, deteriorating school buildings and rising living costs among grievances they share with French students, and a delegation traveled to Paris in solidarity, ANSA reports.

In Ireland, thousands of university students demonstrated in Dublin earlier this month, demanding lower fees, more higher-education funding and affordable accommodation, per RTÉ.

In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions rallied in September to demand greater education investment, more teachers and a more equitable school system, according to Tagesschau.

In Austria, student groups are preparing fresh demonstrations in mid-October after the country's university association warned of possible cuts of around €1 billion from the next three-year university budget, ORF reports.

Between the lines: The education unrest comes as several European governments face mounting pressure to rein in deficits while higher borrowing costs make their debts more expensive to service.

  • France and Belgium are each running budget deficits of more than 5% of their GDP this year, while Austria's is above 4%, according to European Commission forecasts.
  • That squeeze is forcing governments to make difficult choices over public spending.

The bottom line: The protests aren't one coordinated European movement, but students across several countries are mobilizing around their shared concerns.

Go deeper: The global fiscal reckoning is here

item.title: Trump's midterm strategists draw scrutiny over Russia-aligned work
item.description:
President Trump threatened Wednesday to fire two of his top political consultants if he finds a conflict, after reports that they advised a Russia-aligned government ahead of local elections there.

Why it matters: Chris LaCivita and James Blair are leading Republicans' midterm election strategy, putting their foreign consulting work in tension with their prominent roles in Trump's political operation.

What they're saying: Trump called the pair "outside consultants" in a Truth Social post Wednesday.

  • "They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them. They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C."
  • "I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!"

The other side: A source familiar with both consultants and the trip tells Axios that it was "a normal weekend full of calls and texts on the various races and our strategy/tactics in each."

Context: The nationalist party warned that new voting machines could threaten its hold on power, echoing Trump's repeated attacks on voting machines in the U.S.

  • A national election commission required the territory to use the new equipment.
  • The source said Blair and LaCivita were there for about 48 hours to give "strategic advice on Election Integrity and what to look for to spot and avoid potential election fraud, because it was the first election where Republic of Srbska was forced to use new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment…which obviously made them nervous."

Between the lines: Caroline Wren, a registered lobbyist for Srpska, said the republic's abiding interest is in gaining stronger relations with Trump's administration.

  • "It's not about Russia. It's not about Putin. It's about Christians who want their freedom and autonomy," Wren said.
  • "The Trump Administration has made a huge priority of protecting and promoting Christians around the world and there is no better place to do that than the Pro-Trump Christians in the Republic of Sprska who have been demonized by the Europeans and Brussels for their Western values," she said.

Blair and LaCivita were "maybe on the ground for 36 hours," she said, observing that she saw Blair constantly on the phone discussing elections back in the U.S.

  • "Chris and James work around the clock to deliver wins for President Trump and Republicans here at home," she said.

Zoom in: Blair, who previously served as White House deputy chief of staff, left the administration earlier this year to work for MAGA Inc., a super PAC affiliated with the president.

  • He was also a senior adviser on Trump's 2024 campaign. LaCivita, the former co-manager of Trump's 2024 presidential campaign, is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc.

Catch up quick: LaCivita and Blair visited Republika Srpska, a semi-autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of local elections, according to the New York Times.

  • The two were reportedly recruited to advise the government on voting-related issues. They were hired to work for the government, not the nationalist party that controls it, though the party dominates the territory's government.

Yes, but: American political consultants have a long history of taking on foreign clients.

Zoom out: Trump's family businesses have expanded their foreign dealings since he returned to office.

  • The Trump Organization and its partners have more than 20 Trump-branded projects planned, under construction or opening abroad — more than triple the number of overseas properties operating before his return.
  • His administration accepted a luxury Boeing 747 from Qatar slated to eventually go to Trump's presidential library, while a UAE royal-linked firm bought a 49% stake in the Trump family's cryptocurrency business.
  • Donald Trump Jr. had his wedding bankrolled by a Putin-linked Russian oligarch and later repaid him after public outrage.

Go deeper: Trump's presidential profit machine bursts into the open

item.title: Syria considering sending troops to Yemen to fight Houthis
item.description:
Saudi Arabia and Syria are discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to join the counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, three U.S. officials told Axios.

  • Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is seriously considering it, but he hasn't decided.

Why it matters: While the discussion is mostly between Saudi Arabia and Syria, the Trump administration has been consulted by both countries and is not opposed in principle to such a move, the U.S. officials said.

  • But sending Syrian troops could inject a religious dimension into the Yemen war and exacerbate the conflict. The troops could include Islamist Sunni foreign fighters who participated in the rebellion against the Bashar al-Assad regime. They would be fighting against the Houthis, who follow Zaydi Shiite Islam.

Driving the news: The Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a massive ground operation over the weekend against the Houthis. The offensive was designed to retake territories the Houthis control, including the capital Sanaa and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

  • A U.S. official said the issue of sending Syrian troops to Yemen came up during the meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and al-Sharaa in Riyadh earlier this week.
  • The Saudis want al-Sharaa to send troops in order to boost the Yemeni forces that are less trained than the Houthis.
  • While al-Sharaa hasn't signed off on the decision yet, the U.S. official said it is highly likely the Syrian president will accept the Saudi request.

Behind the scenes: The U.S. doesn't oppose sending Syrian troops to Yemen. It would provide more support for the Saudi-backed operation against the Houthis without the U.S. having to get deeply involved, a U.S. official said.

  • Trump administration officials also believe that deploying Syrian troops to Yemen would strengthen the relationship between two U.S. allies, Saudi Arabia and Syria.
  • Two U.S. officials said U.S. Central Command has been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed.
  • The White House and CENTCOM declined to comment. Spokespeople for the Saudi Embassy and the Syrian Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Zoom in: A source with knowledge of the discussions said the Syrian military could send 10,000–20,000 troops to Yemen.

  • The units under consideration are the 90th Division near Damascus and the 84th Division based in southern Syria near Sweida.
  • The 84th Division includes thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who came to Syria during the civil war to fight against the Assad regime under the umbrella of the HTS rebel group.
