item.title: The midterms are an energy election — and here are five places to look
item.description:
Scratch the surface of the year's biggest stories — the Iran war and AI — and both are bound up in the costs of energy.

Why it matters: Prices for gasoline, diesel and power are playing a prominent role in some of the tightest races for control of Congress.

  • The war has kept gasoline prices way above $4 per gallon for months, and helped push diesel to record highs.
  • Fairly or unfairly, data centers are getting blamed for rising electricity prices.
  • It's all unfolding as affordability more broadly tops the agenda in races nationwide.

Here's a look at how energy politics are playing out in five critical contests...

Senate

Michigan. Power prices climbed faster than the national average over the past year in the Wolverine state, and data centers surfaced early in the Democratic primary and stayed prominent in the tight general election race.

  • Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers' campaign shows how Republican hopefuls are willing to split with President Trump on energy and AI — or at least get ahead of him.
  • Rogers called for a one-year moratorium on data centers in August. And he called for a temporary ban on diesel exports in September, an idea Trump then flirted with but backed off.
  • On the Democratic side, if Abdul El-Sayed's January "terms of engagement" for data centers looks familiar, it's because it reflects an increasingly common Democratic view around community buy-in and clean energy.

Ohio. AI's voracious appetite for electricity is fueling the clash between Republican Sen. Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown.

  • Husted has made the case that data centers — not households — should pay for the new power plants and grid infrastructure needed to serve them. A bill he sponsored aimed at doing that fell short in the Senate after passing the House overwhelmingly.
  • Brown is attacking Husted for previously championing data centers and tax incentives to attract them to Ohio.
  • The fight encapsulates a broader question surrounding the AI boom: Who should pay for the massive buildout needed to power it?

Alaska. The Iran war is turning energy prices into a potent issue in the race between Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.

  • In rural communities, fuel already costs far more than in the Lower 48, with gasoline reaching $10 a gallon in some places. Peltola is tying rising fuel costs directly to Sullivan's support for the war, arguing higher diesel prices are hammering fishermen and families.
  • Sullivan has called for temporarily halting U.S. diesel exports and argues Alaska should produce more of its own energy.
  • Looming over it all is Trump's push for a massive Alaska project to export liquefied natural gas.

House

Colorado 8th. This is a contest where energy could be the tipping point. Both general elections in the district's young history have been decided by less than 1%, and energy is prominent this time around.

  • One thing to watch is how much political cover a recent data center vote gives incumbent Republican Gabe Evans.
  • Evans' bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House 417-3 last month. It urges states — but doesn't force them — to set rules ensuring data center developers cover generation and grid upgrade costs.
  • Don't sleep on gasoline either. New Democratic ads supporting challenger Manny Rutinel tie Evans to Trump's war with Iran and higher gasoline prices.

Pennsylvania 8th. Data centers have become a central issue in the House race between Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan and Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti.

  • Northeastern Pennsylvania is fielding proposals for the energy-hungry facilities. Cognetti is campaigning explicitly against projects that raise electric bills, threaten water supplies or receive tax breaks.
  • Bresnahan, who has previously supported data center development, has introduced legislation aimed at protecting local governments that reject projects from corporate lawsuits.
  • The fight captures the emerging politics around AI infrastructure: Communities may want the investment and jobs, but they also want control over the costs.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Trump has a new target: The words Americans use
item.description:
President Trump has long nicknamed his opponents, and now, as November approaches, he's even trying to dictate the vocabulary around key issues.

The big picture: Trump's latest effort to reshape political language follows his longtime political strategy: Define the terms of the debate, and you gain power over the debate itself.

  • But as polling on those issues continues to haunt the president's party, Trump's new vocabulary may not be enough to change voters' minds.

Case in point: Americans are worried about AI — but to Trump, that word no longer exists. It's "super intelligence" now.

  • Voters are also concerned about affordability, but that's a "new word" and a "hoax," Trump says.
  • And the war in Iran? Sometimes Trump says it's a war — a word that carries strict legal implications — and other times it's an "excursion," a "military operation" or a "skirmish."

The intrigue: The issues are starkly different, but the throughline is the way Trump frames the linguistic building blocks of political debate.

  • "If you can actually get everyone who influences our perception of language to adopt your language, you have a very powerful capacity," says Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a communications professor at the University of Pennsylvania and director emerita of the Annenberg Public Policy Center.

What they're saying: "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to Axios.

The latest: As fears about AI's potential threat to humanity (which the president has labeled a "hoax") boiled over, Trump — who has favored a light regulatory touch — signed an executive order replacing "artificial" with a different word: "super."

  • "This is a highly contentious issue right now that is working against him because his position is unpopular," Jamieson says.
  • She adds: "But AI … is so pervasive right now in the news environment and the anxieties of the culture that if you can attach positive affect to it as opposed to negative affect to it, you've accomplished something."
  • The reaction has been mixed: Elon Musk said he'd rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, but Sam Altman told Politico he wouldn't rename OpenAI, noting that "brands are sticky."

Zoom in: Trump is also fighting an uphill battle against the word "affordability": a simple term for complex economic strain that Democrats harnessed in key elections and have championed throughout the midterm cycle.

  • He's said it's a word the press devised, a "fake word" and a Democratic "con job." But unlike with SI, he hasn't offered an alternative.
  • But he's also leaned on his own midterm buzz words, "communism" being a prime example.

Between the lines: "If you can shape which words are used in a political debate and how those words are defined, then you've won the debate before it even starts," explains Jennifer Mercieca, a Texas A&M professor and author of "Demagogue for President: The Rhetorical Genius of Donald Trump."

  • "President Trump knows this, of course, and has been very successful in re-framing or re-defining issues," she writes to Axios, pointing to his popularization of the term "fake news." But Trump's "frame warfare isn't surprising" as "it is essential to how politics works today."
  • Trump's second administration has expanded that battle over language, renaming the Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario and the Department of Defense. Keywords tied to diversity and gender have driven grant cancellations.
  • And with Trump's punitive response to anyone who doesn't use his preferred language, Jamieson says: "You may be adding a function to the presidency, a controversial function, which is namer-in-chief."

The bottom line: Our perceptions can be shaped by language — but the key question for November is whether our elections can be.

Go deeper: Inside Trump's "super intelligence" naming problem

item.title: Missing details keep U.S. plague response on hold
item.description:
Two big unknowns stand in the way of determining how serious the plague threat in Russia is and whether travel advisories, restrictions at U.S. ports of entry or other precautions are warranted.

  • We still don't know which pathogen killed a Russian researcher, or how well contained it is.

Why it matters: Though public health experts say there's no cause for Americans to panic, the episode serves as a wake-up call emphasizing the nature of global biological threats and the need for pandemic preparedness.

State of play: A worker at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East recently died after contracting pneumonia. There are conflicting accounts of how she got sick and whether she was infected with pneumonic plague, which is almost always deadly without prompt treatment with antibiotics.

  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration is closely monitoring the situation, adding, "I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on. And we're doing that."
  • If a response is required, "the playbook for these instances is very well defined," David Mansdoerfer, a former health official in the first Trump administration, told Axios.
  • "Traditionally, the precautionary measures the government would take would be via a travel advisory from [the State Department]," he said, adding the U.S. already has its most serious travel warning in place for Russia due to the war with Ukraine.
  • It would also contact U.S. citizens in the affected area with guidance, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would follow up with a travel health notice, Mansdoerfer said.
  • "The government would then focus on [Customs and Border Protection] ill traveler rules" that can include stopping high-risk individuals from boarding flights or flagging health officials if they land at a port of entry. At that point, "it becomes a CDC protocol-driven process," he added.

The intrigue: If the Russian worker did die from pneumonic plague, experts say there's a possibility that it was a genetically altered version that behaves differently than the treatable strain.

  • That's just speculation at this point. But the prevalence of "gain-of-function" research that enhances pathogens to study them and Russia's known development of biological weapons make it impossible to rule out.

U.S. preparedness efforts will focus first on getting as much detailed information as possible because officials first need to understand what is going on to prepare for it, said Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

  • "It's really critical to get the diagnosis right. There are conflicting stories around it," Inglesby said, noting that while there are substantial supplies of antibiotics in government stockpiles and pharmacies, there's still the possibility the strain is resistant to them.

Another key unknown is if pneumonia believed to be linked to plague has spread in the community. So far, reports suggest it's limited to the lab scientist who died while others in the community are under close monitoring. 

  • "Pneumonic plague does not normally cause large outbreaks in modern times, it happens rarely but it's very uncommon," Inglesby said. "If many people in that city do get sick, that would call into question the diagnosis, or raise concerns about something else going on."
  • "Getting the real story, the true facts of the situation out in the open is critical to everything else that follows in the response," he added.

Asked whether he's concerned, President Trump on Monday said: "Somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They're like an army ... even with great advances, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don't work as well anymore."

Friction point: Determining whether the incident resulted from legitimate plague research as opposed to a weapons program is important, considering the still-heated debate over COVID's origins and the Russian institute's connection with the nation's biowarfare apparatus.

  • There's no credible evidence that the deceased worker at the Russian institute was involved with research on a weaponized or engineered strain. In fact, some reports state she had recently traveled to regions along the Mongolia-Russia border, where plague naturally occurs in animals.
  • The institute where she worked was established as part of an anti-plague network and was mainly responsible for surveillance of dangerous pathogens. But it developed vaccines and diagnostics for pathogens that were modified by the military, according to the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies.

A 2024 State Department assessment concluded Russia maintains an offensive bioweapons program and absorbed the old Soviet program and evolved it.

  • The CDC says the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s manufactured large quantities of antibiotic-resistant Y. pestis [the bacteria that causes plague] to be dispersed in the air as a bioweapon and that, in light of these and recent events involving terrorist organizations, the United States and other countries must be prepared for a bioterrorism attack involving Y. pestis.

Zoom out: Pneumonic plague cases are rare but not unheard of, including in the U.S.

  • Last year, the CDC launched a pneumonic plague investigation in Arizona after a young adult male died after exposure to two ill cats. Officials identified 46 potentially exposed persons, who were given antibiotics.

The bottom line: In the most optimistic scenario, Russia has responded with an abundance of caution to a one-off deadly infection that hasn't spread.

  • But there's too much that still needs to be verified to draw any conclusions.
item.content:encoded:
Two big unknowns stand in the way of determining how serious the plague threat in Russia is and whether travel advisories, restrictions at U.S. ports of entry or other precautions are warranted.

  • We still don't know which pathogen killed a Russian researcher, or how well contained it is.

Why it matters: Though public health experts say there's no cause for Americans to panic, the episode serves as a wake-up call emphasizing the nature of global biological threats and the need for pandemic preparedness.

State of play: A worker at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East recently died after contracting pneumonia. There are conflicting accounts of how she got sick and whether she was infected with pneumonic plague, which is almost always deadly without prompt treatment with antibiotics.

  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration is closely monitoring the situation, adding, "I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on. And we're doing that."
  • If a response is required, "the playbook for these instances is very well defined," David Mansdoerfer, a former health official in the first Trump administration, told Axios.
  • "Traditionally, the precautionary measures the government would take would be via a travel advisory from [the State Department]," he said, adding the U.S. already has its most serious travel warning in place for Russia due to the war with Ukraine.
  • It would also contact U.S. citizens in the affected area with guidance, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would follow up with a travel health notice, Mansdoerfer said.
  • "The government would then focus on [Customs and Border Protection] ill traveler rules" that can include stopping high-risk individuals from boarding flights or flagging health officials if they land at a port of entry. At that point, "it becomes a CDC protocol-driven process," he added.

The intrigue: If the Russian worker did die from pneumonic plague, experts say there's a possibility that it was a genetically altered version that behaves differently than the treatable strain.

  • That's just speculation at this point. But the prevalence of "gain-of-function" research that enhances pathogens to study them and Russia's known development of biological weapons make it impossible to rule out.

U.S. preparedness efforts will focus first on getting as much detailed information as possible because officials first need to understand what is going on to prepare for it, said Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

  • "It's really critical to get the diagnosis right. There are conflicting stories around it," Inglesby said, noting that while there are substantial supplies of antibiotics in government stockpiles and pharmacies, there's still the possibility the strain is resistant to them.

Another key unknown is if pneumonia believed to be linked to plague has spread in the community. So far, reports suggest it's limited to the lab scientist who died while others in the community are under close monitoring. 

  • "Pneumonic plague does not normally cause large outbreaks in modern times, it happens rarely but it's very uncommon," Inglesby said. "If many people in that city do get sick, that would call into question the diagnosis, or raise concerns about something else going on."
  • "Getting the real story, the true facts of the situation out in the open is critical to everything else that follows in the response," he added.

Asked whether he's concerned, President Trump on Monday said: "Somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They're like an army ... even with great advances, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don't work as well anymore."

Friction point: Determining whether the incident resulted from legitimate plague research as opposed to a weapons program is important, considering the still-heated debate over COVID's origins and the Russian institute's connection with the nation's biowarfare apparatus.

But it developed vaccines and diagnostics for pathogens that were modified by the military, according to the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies.

A 2024 State Department assessment concluded Russia maintains an offensive bioweapons program and absorbed the old Soviet program and evolved it.

item.title: Scoop: Senate GOP to send $5m to shore up Graham in South Carolina
item.description:
The main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates plans to inject $5 million into the South Carolina campaign as an "insurance policy" to help GOP nominee Darline Graham, a source familiar with the move tells Axios.

Why it matters: The GOP's concern that a Senate seat in blood-red South Carolina could be in play shows just how bad the political environment is for Republicans, who face a rash of troubles in states long considered conservative strongholds.

  • "It's an insurance policy. We're going to be there for Darline," said a Republican briefed on the plans for the Senate Leadership Fund.

The shift to spending in conservative South Carolina comes after Senate Republicans announced they no longer were financing ads in swing-state North Carolina, where the GOP's Michael Whatley is lagging behind former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in polls.

  • Democrats, meanwhile, are reallocating resources in a way that reflects their optimism four weeks before Election Day.
  • Democrats' main Senate super PAC canceled roughly $1.1 million in ad reservations in North Carolina, Semafor reported, based on their belief Cooper is well-positioned to flip the seat now held by retiring Republican Thom Tillis.

Zoom in: Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was appointed to her seat in July at the urging of President Trump, a friend of her brother's. Graham faces a host of challenges:

  • She's a relatively poor fundraiser compared to her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who is outspending and outraising Graham, according to the South Carolina Post & Courier.
  • Unlike her brother, Graham shields herself from the press and has shown a relative lack of mastery of foreign policy, which tripped her up during a GOP primary debate.
  • Graham won that primary over Rep. Ralph Norman with 52% of the vote after getting help from Trump. It left some bad feelings with Norman, who endorsed her but briefly suggested he would mount a write-in campaign for the Nov. 3 general election.

Zoom out: Voter anger over high prices and Trump's sagging popularity have helped to create a political landscape in which the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC is having to play defense across the country.

  • It's trying to shore up GOP incumbents and challengers from Alaska to Ohio to Texas, where it recently plowed in $131 million over 17 days to boost Ken Paxton's campaign against Democrat James Talarico.
  • "We're not taking anything for granted. We won't be caught flat-footed in any of these races," the source said.
  • The money for Graham will be spent mainly on TV ads to "remind voters that Andrews is a Democrat."
  • Democrats haven't won a statewide race in South Carolina since 2006.

By the numbers: Closer-than-expected polling from two firms that typically survey for Republicans sparked concern last week in GOP circles.

  • A survey from Trafalgar showed Graham pulling 43% and Andrews 42%, a statistical tie.
  • InsiderAdvantage also produced a poll showing a 1-point race that's essentially tied, with Graham at 46% and Andrews at 45%.
  • Earlier in September, GOP-leaning Rasmussen Reports showed Graham up by 5 points.

Catch up quick: Andrews' campaign has been under the radar compared to that of Jaime Harrison, the Democrat who challenged Graham's brother for the seat in 2020.

  • Harrison raised $100 million for that race, but because he was the state's former Democratic Party chair, it was easier for Republicans to make the race a partisan contest.
  • In contrast, Andrews is running as a "mom and a doctor." Her campaign was largely financed with $3.6 million in campaign contributions bundled by 314 Action Fund, a political committee founded to elect Democratic candidates with STEM backgrounds.

What they're saying: "South Carolinians don't know who Darline Graham is or what she believes — she avoids reporters, avoids voters, and lies about Annie rather than doing her job," an Andrews spokesperson told Axios.

  • A Graham spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
  • Trump gave a preview Monday of the bare-knuckle attacks to come when he took to Truth Social and used a slur for transgender people to attack Andrews while accusing her of a host of liberal positions.
  • "South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her," Trump wrote.

The 314 Action Fund jabbed back at the president in a statement late Monday, calling Trump "perverted" and saying that he "has resorted to name-calling and juvenile insults because his candidate can't win on the issues."

Axios' Hans Nichols contributed to this story.

item.title: Longevity guru Bryan Johnson: "People really want me to die"
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Bryan Johnson, the face of the longevity movement who believes he may never die, announced recently that he had an incurable autoimmune disease — and his critics cheered, he told "The Axios Show" in an exclusive interview Monday.

  • "I mean, I think people really want me to die. Now I get it. It's funny. It's ironic. I push a lot of buttons that people don't like," he said.

The big picture: As Johnson himself acknowledged, there's an irony in the founder of the "Don't Die" movement watching people celebrate his diagnosis. But Johnson sees his diagnosis as rocket fuel for his mission to promote longevity, rather than a setback.

Catch up quick: Johnson, 49, has autoimmune gastritis (AIG), a chronic condition in which the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach lining.

  • Johnson said "there was joy all around the world" after he announced his diagnosis in July.
  • He spends millions of dollars a year on extreme health interventions, documenting the experiments for an online following that has ballooned to roughly 8 million across platforms including YouTube.
  • When asked if any of his interventions could have fueled his AIG diagnosis, he said: "No. I got diagnosed with hypothyroidism when I was 21 years old. The thyroid and the stomach are very closely linked in immunology. I probably have had this thing for about 30 years."

The intrigue: Johnson views the diagnosis, which might appear to undermine his campaign against aging, as just another test of it.

  • In his view, his efforts to do more than manage the disease can help prove the efficacy of his ambitions.
  • "I like the challenge. I'm up for it. I think it's good timing. I'm going to get diagnosed with something at some point. Why not this?"

Friction point: Johnson, who calls himself the "most measured person in the world," spends over $2 million a year on his personal health and longevity treatments. He has an entire medical concierge team and a makeshift doctor's office in his home.

  • Experts say the cause of the disease is unknown, and that Johnson's proposed effort to reverse it is experimental.

Zoom out: Johnson made his fortune founding Braintree, which bought Venmo and was later sold to PayPal for $800 million.

  • He now runs longevity businesses including Blueprint and Immortals, alongside neurotechnology company Kernel and venture fund OS Fund.

Between the lines: One common critique of intensive health tracking is that more testing can uncover more abnormalities, not all of them meaningful.

  • Doctors warn that false positives and incidental findings can trigger a "cascade" of follow-up tests and treatments that can bring added cost, stress, and in some cases, harm.

Johnson is a full-throated fan: "I personally appreciate information. I want to know because when you find things early, you're much more likely to be able to address them."

  • He also said his process doesn't feel addictive to him, adding that "the biggest addiction in the world is to make money."

The bottom line: The face of the longevity movement sees the hit to his public health record as another potential achievement in his quest to live forever.

item.title: Wall Street on track for record profits
item.description:
Data: NYSE/Intercontinental Exchange via the New York State Comptroller; Chart Emily Peck/Axios; Note: 2026 projected by the comptroller if first-half growth continues at current pace. First-half 2026 profits were $45.9 billion. Profits are for broker-dealer operations of NYSE member firms and are not adjusted for inflation.

Wall Street profits are blowing past expectations this year, the New York State Comptroller's office finds in a new report.

Why it matters: Profits are on track for an all-time record, a sign of how the AI boom is fueling dealmaking and how volatile markets are helping trading.

By the numbers: In the first half of this year, Wall Street firms raked in $45.9 billion — that's 51.3% more than the same period last year, and already more than the $45.3 billion forecast for the entirety of 2026.

  • If growth continues apace, annual profits could exceed $90 billion.

Zoom out: That's far more than 2025's record $65.1 billion and rivals the 2009 record even after accounting for inflation, the report says.

Stunning stat: The fees that firms earn from underwriting — helping companies sell new stocks and bonds — rose 68% in the first half of the year, compared with the first half of 2025.

Zoom in: That tracks with a 76.5% increase in global equity issuance, a large chunk from the SpaceX initial public offering.

  • Plus, there was also an 11.3% increase in debt issuance, with the AI hyperscalers among the biggest borrowers.

Yes, but: It's anyone's guess as to whether the second half of the year looks like the first.

  • There are plenty of market headwinds blowing: the Iran war, higher inflation and interest rates, the potential for the AI bubble to burst among them.

The intrigue: Wall Street appears to be thriving despite fears over the city's democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

The big picture: The securities industry makes up a big and growing share of the city and state's tax revenues, but local business and politics aren't significant profit engines.

  • Those instead are driven by national and global markets — it's been a huge year for stocks, the SpaceX IPO was the biggest ever, M&A hit a record and war-driven volatility juiced trading.

What to watch: The big Wall Street banks are set to release third-quarter earnings numbers next week — that's the first big test of whether the pace is holding up.

item.title: Latino group bets on bilingual AI to cut voter confusion before the midterms
item.description:
A national Latino civic engagement group is turning to an AI app to help voters cut through an increasingly complicated election system — in English or Spanish.

Why it matters: Nearly 39 million Hispanics can vote in this year's midterms, and their political loyalties are increasingly up for grabs.

  • Hispanics have added 5.25 million eligible voters since 2022, more than any other racial or ethnic group, according to Pew Research Center.
  • The Latino electorate remains highly fluid: About 1 in 7 Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 now say they want Democrats to control Congress, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll.

How it works: Mi Familia en Acción launched Nubi last week, a bilingual AI-powered app that answers questions about voting, voter registration, citizenship and Know Your Rights information.

  • Users can ask questions in English or Spanish about where and when to vote, early voting, mail ballots and registration.
  • Nubi operates in all 50 states and can tailor information to the local or district level.

Unlike a general-purpose chatbot, Mi Familia en Acción president and CEO Héctor Sánchez Barba tells Axios that Nubi doesn't search the open internet for answers.

  • The organization feeds it information from sources it considers reliable, with human review and guardrails around what the AI can answer.
  • If Nubi doesn't have an answer, Sánchez said, it is designed to say so and direct the user to a trusted source or partner rather than invent a response.

State of play: Nubi represents a five-year effort to marry Mi Familia en Acción's traditional organizing with technology.

  • The organization launched a more basic chatbot about two years ago before developing the current AI version.
  • Mi Familia en Acción financed development itself, Sánchez said, though he declined to disclose the cost, calling it a "very big investment."
  • The organization says it plans to keep updating Nubi as voting rules, court decisions and government policies change.

Zoom in: The goal is to turn a complicated search across election websites into a conversation.

  • A voter could ask whether they're registered, whether they can vote by mail, where their polling place is or what early-voting options exist.
  • Nubi then walks the user through basic questions before giving a locally specific answer.
  • The tool is updated regularly and eventually could expand its answers on questions involving immigration enforcement or problems a voter encounters at a polling place.

What they're saying: "People don't need to be a constitutional lawyer to find information about how they need to vote," said Sánchez, adding that the goal is to put reliable information in one place.

  • He stressed that Nubi is nonpartisan and doesn't recommend candidates or causes.
  • Sánchez also said the technology won't replace door-knocking and other traditional organizing, but could extend civic information into rural or overlooked communities that organizers rarely reach.

Zoom out: Nubi arrives as Latino voters play an increasingly large — and less predictable — role in American elections.

  • Pew projects Hispanics will account for 16% of eligible voters in 2026, nearly double their 9% share in 2006.
  • Latino voters are also fragmenting into competing political identities rather than moving uniformly toward either party.
  • In May, 52% of registered Latino voters surveyed in 17 competitive House districts said they were undecided or could change their minds.

  • Pew projects Hispanics will account for 16% of eligible voters in 2026, nearly double their 9% share in 2006.
  • Latino voters are also fragmenting into competing political identities rather than moving uniformly toward either party.
  • In May, 52% of registered Latino voters surveyed in 17 competitive House districts said they were undecided or could change their minds.

item.title: Scoop: Gun safety groups jump into midterms with $10 million assist for Democrats
item.description:
Everytown for Gun Safety, a group that advocates for stricter gun laws, is teaming up with House Democrats on a $10 million ad campaign to boost former gun safety advocates now running for Congress, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: That's a significant sum at a moment when Democrats are raising alarm bells about being outgunned financially in the midterm elections.

  • The candidates boosted by the campaign are all former volunteers for Moms Demand Action, which is part of Everytown.
  • The candidates include: JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, Pia Dandiya of Florida, Christina Bohannan, Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James of Iowa, Christina Hines and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, and Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania.

"For nearly two years, a MAGA House has rubber-stamped the Trump administration as it tore up federal gun safety laws, and flipping these eight seats is how we put a stop to it," Everytown president John Feinblatt said in a statement first shared with Axios.

  • "There's a Moms Demand Action volunteer on the ballot in every one of these districts, and we're partnering with House Majority PAC to turn them into majority makers."
  • Mike Smith, the president of House Democrats' main super PAC, House Majority PAC, said in a statement: "Every seat on this map is a chance to put a check on a Trump administration and a MAGA House that have spent two years putting the gun lobby ahead of American families."

Between the lines: The money will go to fund TV and digital ads focused broadly on "public safety," referencing not just gun control but drug trafficking, immigration, crime, and police funding.

  • The Bohannan ad says she is "running for Congress to put public safety first. That means working with both parties to secure our border, hire more police officers and keep illegal guns and fentanyl off our streets."
  • The Cognetti ad mostly focuses on her broader anti-corruption message but lauds how "she got millions for police and cut violent crime by 80%" as mayor of Scranton.

The other side: "House Democrats have fully embraced the radical socialist agenda of abolishing prisons, releasing criminals back on the streets, and defunding the police," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement.

  • "Voters won't buy their lies about Republicans who have fought to protect our communities."

Editor's note: This article has been corrected to clarify that Moms Demand Action is part of Everytown.

item.title: Inside Trump's new AI playbook
item.description:
President Trump's newly minted "super intelligence" task force faces a daunting mandate: Reconcile fiercely divided Cabinet factions to create a tech policy that keeps pace with the blistering AI race.

Why it matters: The task force brings the administration's scattered AI work under one roof, but it also makes it likely that any new rules will be forged in the crossfire of competing internal camps.

  • In an interview, task force co-chair Scott Kupor rejected the assertion that the administration is asleep at the wheel on AI policy, arguing that rigid, static legislation would risk becoming instantly obsolete.

What they're saying: "The worst thing for us to do would be to assume a static set of knowledge that allows us to put a regulatory schema in place that then has unintended consequences," said Kupor, a Silicon Valley veteran who is currently serving as director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, akin to an HR director for the federal government.

  • "Look, we live in D.C.," he said. "There's nothing that's not political in this town. People have different views and that's totally fine. Our obligation is to demonstrate to the American people that this is good and also that we take the anxieties and the concerns seriously."
  • "At the end of the day there is no daylight between the president and anyone else ... we need to win," he said.

Between the lines: The group's makeup highlights the competing fiefdoms driving Trump's AI strategy, with some working on model approval and coordination and others continuing to voice deep skepticism about pro-regulation forces in the industry.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trump Chief of Staff Susie Wiles have worked behind the scenes to encourage some oversight, including through the voluntary model-review process that already exists.
  • Managed within the Commerce Department, the reviews have already been used for top models at Anthropic, OpenAI and now Google, sources tell Axios.
  • On the other end of the spectrum, figures like David Sacks and the Pentagon's Emil Michael represent an approach that is wary of the potential for a slowdown in model development or new regulation to reduce competition for frontier companies.
  • Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and the new AI czar, is expected to bring cohesion to the group's collective work, much as he does with the myriad intelligence agencies.

The entire committee is set to operate under Trump's explicit marching orders: Innovation cannot be bottlenecked, and America must stay ahead while finding a safe path forward, Kupor said.

  • Kupor suggested one outcome may be that AI regulation is divided among different federal agencies, although it is too early to know what the group — which will do its work over 120 days — will ultimately recommend to the president.
  • His primary area of focus initially will be to seek input from stakeholders in the energy, manufacturing, security and financial services industries. Kupor said he expects Clayton will keep close tabs on the intelligence community and the committee will continue to stay in close touch with the AI companies.

Zoom in: The administration is leaning hard into corporate self-policing to manage the risks. Kupor and other officials believe that third-party audits and direct reporting to corporate boards carry severe securities law implications that rival traditional government oversight.

The bottom line: The task force's goal isn't to draft a bureaucratic "Ph.D. dissertation," in Kupor's words. But it remains to be seen whether streamlining existing efforts without new legislation will satisfy Americans who are increasingly anxious about AI safety.

item.title: The most-watched election in U.S. history
item.description:
The 2026 midterms are shaping up to be the most intensely observed, recorded, dissected and challenged election in American history.

Why it matters: A small army of partisan and nonpartisan observers will show up. So will a surge of Justice Department monitors, organizers looking for signs of ICE and citizen journalists broadcasting their search for illegal voting in real time.

Between the lines: More nonpartisan observation can bolster confidence in elections, studies show. But officials worry that activists expecting to find wrongdoing could misread routine events.

  • Election officials have been raising concerns that "vigilante citizen journalists" could interfere with the election, said Andrew Walchuck of Common Cause, a nonprofit organization that's also recruiting nonpartisan election observers.
  • "I worry that people are going to go in and claim they're seeing things that they aren't," said Andrew Garber of the Brennan Center.
  • "Just minor, innocuous things that are going to happen as millions and millions of ballots get cast and counted, then it gets spun into something nefarious or untrue," Garber said.

The intrigue: After the 2020 election, claims from observers and activist sleuths helped fuel challenges to the results.

  • It was then channeled into numerous lawsuits from the Trump campaign. The cases were almost all dismissed or denied relief in court.

Influencers and online activists can turn real-time claims about wrongdoing into national controversy before officials can weigh in or push back — including while votes are being cast or counted.

  • "What gives me concern is that we have an administration that is trying to spread conspiracy theories and spread lies about our elections and... [then] having more people out there with that purpose behind their work troubles me," Walchuck said.

The other side: "Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of voter fraud continues to pile up. Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable," Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement.

  • This year there have been more than two dozen federal charges against people for voting when they're not eligible and about 160 arrests, according to the Justice Department.
  • A review from the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonpartisan organization, says instances of illegal voting are "extremely small."

Zoom in: The DOJ plans to train 1,000 election monitors to deploy across the country, one of the largest-ever efforts from the agency. It builds on a significant increase in observers in 2024.

  • The Senate Democrats have spun up their own arm of election observers, using office staff to monitor the polls. That's in addition to a new 50-state-plus-territories recruitment program by a coalition of Democratic state parties, aiming to recruit at least 10,000 election watchers.
  • The Republican National Committee is building on its election watch network set up in 2020 to counter perceived voter fraud. GOP partisans have signed up in record numbers to be poll workers and the party is hosting virtual and in-person trainings for observers and challengers.
  • A network of anti-ICE activists is transitioning ICE watch trainings into poll watching trainings, responding in part to the Trump administration saying ICE could make arrests at the polls. When asked in September about deploying agents, Trump told TIME magazine he hadn't thought of it.

Zoom out: These efforts will coexist with a slew of nonpartisan observing efforts, ranging from voter protection groups to international election observers.

  • There will also be state party and campaign staffers who regularly monitor the polls for concerns. These are typically more mundane, including monitoring accurate opening and closing times for polling locations that can be remedied with quick litigation.
  • The rules and terminology for observers vary by state laws, which also govern how close an observer can be to voting machines or tabulation processes and how to document concerns about malpractice.

The bottom line: "Having questions and wanting to understand more about the election process as a sort of curious citizen is a good thing," said Avery Davis-Roberts of the Carter Center, which monitors elections internationally and will have volunteers in five states in November.

  • "And we hope that people will use observation and the findings of our observation as a way to better understand how the process works and maybe have some of those questions answered."

item.title: Inside the transgender rights fight injecting chaos into Democrats' midterm efforts
item.description:
An intra-party debate over how best to deflect Republican attacks on transgender issues has Democrats angrily sniping at each other just weeks out from the midterm elections.

Why it matters: This is not the position Democrats hoped to be in two years after their 2024 election loss, which many in the party attributed to being outflanked by GOP messaging on trans issues.

  • "People feel you need to respond in some way to some of these attacks because people didn't do it two years ago," Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a co-chair of the Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus, told Axios.
  • "But you also need to realize what we're winning on right now," Pocan added, saying Democratic candidates need to strike "a balance."
  • "Silence is deadly, and I think we played that out in 2024," said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at the centrist think tank Third Way, citing polling that found most voters believed Democrats "thought there should be no rules in sports, no rules around health care."

Driving the news: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) set off a firestorm in her district and on Capitol Hill in September by stating in a direct-to-camera ad that she "voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools."

  • "Parents know what's best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls' sports," Kaptur said in the spot — a response to an ad from Republican Derek Merrin that said she "voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports."
  • Multiple county parties condemned the ad — particularly the reference to transgender girls as "boys" — and urged Kaptur to take it down.
  • One LGBTQ+ group, the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, said in a statement there is "no difference" between Kaptur and Merrin because they are "both united against the LBTQIA+ community."

What they're saying: "The ads were deeply offensive to the Equality Caucus and the broader LGBTQ community that we represent," said Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.), who co-chairs the caucus' political arm, Equality PAC.

  • He told Axios: "The Equality Caucus is not going to stand by passively and allow anyone to scapegoat the trans community. It is a red line for us."
  • Equality PAC "is absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time," the group said in a separate statement to Axios, calling Kaptur's language "unacceptable."

What we're hearing: Kaptur's colleagues also privately communicated their disgust with the ad to her office, multiple House Democrats familiar with the matter told Axios.

  • The lawmakers predicted there will be in-person conversations with Kaptur when the House returns in November, especially if she wins her election.
  • "Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls' sports stay fair," said Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer.
  • "She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor."

Zoom out: It's not just Kaptur. Democratic House candidates Blake Gendebien of New York and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa, and Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, have put out ads featuring similar rhetoric.

  • Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) released an ad last week in which he said there are "real concerns about fairness and safety" and that "states should decide what's right for protecting women and girls."
  • That ad, like Kaptur's, raised eyebrows privately among LGBTQ+ House Democrats, though none have called him out publicly for it.

The other side: Centrist groups and lawmakers say the party has to be realistic about districts like Kaptur's, which President Trump carried by 11 percentage points in 2024.

  • "Marcy Kaptur and Don Davis are doing the most important work in Democratic politics: winning Trump districts," said Liam Kerr, cofounder of centrist group Welcome PAC.
  • Kerr argued attacks from LGBTQ+ groups will only help swing-district Democrats: "Taking the 20% side of an 80/20 issue may be bad politics, but elevating the big winners repudiating you is even worse advocacy."

Between the lines: "Our latest [research] showed that anti-trans attacks take about 8 points off of the Democratic vote if you just let it sit out there," Erickson, the Third Way official, told Axios.

  • "But there are ways to respond that get you back up 10 to 12 to 14 points," she continued. "There are a bunch of different ways to say it ... just being clear that there need to be rules. Not laws, but rules."
  • "When it comes to health care, that parents, not politicians, should be in charge of decisions about their kids' health care."

The bottom line: Centrists and LGBTQ+ Democrats alike say a careful balance can and should be struck.

  • Several lawmakers pointed to Senate hopefuls James Talarico and Sherrod Brown as examples for deftly maneuvering on this issue.
  • Erickson said "calling transgender girls 'boys' ... is not respectful" and that candidates "don't have to do it. There's better ways to talk about this."

item.title: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base because of threat of Iranian drone attack
item.description:
The U.S. military evacuated a dozen B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the UK over the weekend as a result of intelligence suggesting an Iranian drone attack, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: Such an Iranian drone attack from British soil against the base could have led to the killing of U.S. service members and destroyed the strategic bombers.

  • It would have been an unprecedented and brazen attack by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential for dramatic escalation in the war in the Middle East.
  • When asked by reporters on Monday if Iran planned to launch a drone attack against the base from British soil, Trump said: "I can't tell you that. If they did they will suffer greatly."

Driving the news: The dozen B-1 bombers were evacuated from the base in the UK only several weeks after being deployed there.

  • The Pentagon said on Sunday that "all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States."
  • It added that the U.S. military bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, "remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States."

Between the lines: The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base.

  • U.S. officials say it is unclear whether the people who were arrested are connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack.

Behind the scenes: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel gave the UK intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack.

  • On Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Netanyahu from the plane on his way to Iceland, the State Department said.

What they're saying: Rubio told reporters earlier that the movement of the bombers was part of "regular rotations" of U.S. Air Force assets around the world and was not directly tied to an Iranian threat.

  • But several hours later, President Trump contradicted Rubio and told reporters the bombers were moved because of a security threat from Iran.
  • "They didn't fly out by accident ... there was a threat. We moved them around a little bit," he said.
  • Trump added that the U.S. knows who was behind the threat and their links to Iran.
  • Trump was then asked about the attempted terrorist attack on the Fly Dubai flight and said he thinks Iran was responsible.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. military evacuated a dozen B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the UK over the weekend as a result of intelligence suggesting an Iranian drone attack, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: Such an Iranian drone attack from British soil against the base could have led to the killing of U.S. service members and destroyed the strategic bombers.

  • It would have been an unprecedented and brazen attack by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential for dramatic escalation in the war in the Middle East.
  • When asked by reporters on Monday if Iran planned to launch a drone attack against the base from British soil, Trump said: "I can't tell you that. If they did they will suffer greatly."

Driving the news: The dozen B-1 bombers were evacuated from the base in the UK only several weeks after being deployed there.

  • The Pentagon said on Sunday that "all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States."
  • It added that the U.S. military bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, "remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States."

Between the lines: The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base.

  • U.S. officials say it is unclear whether the people who were arrested are connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack.

Behind the scenes: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel gave the UK intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack.

  • On Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Netanyahu from the plane on his way to Iceland, the State Department said.

What they're saying: Rubio told reporters earlier that the movement of the bombers was part of "regular rotations" of U.S. Air Force assets around the world and was not directly tied to an Iranian threat.

  • But several hours later, President Trump contradicted Rubio and told reporters the bombers were moved because of a security threat from Iran.
  • "They didn't fly out by accident ... there was a threat. We moved them around a little bit," he said.
  • Trump added that the U.S. knows who was behind the threat and their links to Iran.
  • Trump was then asked about the attempted terrorist attack on the Fly Dubai flight and said he thinks Iran was responsible.
item.dc:creator: Barak Ravid

item.title: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
item.description:
President Trump said Monday that the United States will help Russia amid a potential case of pneumonic plague, though he hasn't spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it.

Why it matters: International concern spiked over the weekend over the news that a Russian lab worker had died from a possible case of pneumonic plague, reminding some of how the COVID-19 epidemic began.

Trump's comments came after a question about the reported death of Darya Shipilova, who was potentially exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia.

  • There has been no official confirmation that Shipilova's death was due to pneumonic plague, but five hospitals in the area and dozens of institute workers have been quarantined out of precaution.
  • Russian health authorities say Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing showed no pathogen tied to her work.
  • No additional deaths or sicknesses tied to the incident have been reported.

What they're saying: "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday.

  • "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can."
  • Trump said the disease used to be more controllable, but "microbes and the germs have gotten stronger."
  • The president appeared to be referring to antimicrobial resistance, but pneumonic plague itself remains treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early

Between the lines: The White House is monitoring the outbreak, Axios scooped, with the Department of Health and Human Services and State Department also on alert.

  • The European Commission is also "very closely" monitoring the suspected outbreak.

Go deeper: How pneumonic plague spreads, and how it is and isn't like COVID

item.title: How states are tackling midterm pump pain
item.description:
States are taking on the stubbornly high fuel prices squeezing Americans ahead of the midterm elections, pushing through tax holidays and other tactics to offer relief while federal efforts have stalled.

Why it matters: With November 3 less than 30 days away, the political stakes of those price-lowering levers — even if the relief is only modest — are surging amid sky-high costs.

  • While several lawmakers have introduced legislation aimed at or pressed for suspending the federal gas tax, which is 18.4 cents per gallon for gas and 24.4 for diesel, Washington hasn't coalesced around a solution.

Driving the news: That's left states seeking ways to give their residents relief.

Case in point: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) signed a bill last week that suspends Ohio's gas tax for 90 days, an effort that earned bipartisan backing.

  • There's an underlying election story: The state's Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, had called for a gas tax holiday, followed by her rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, announcing a plan with GOP leaders.

Flashback: Georgia was the first state to suspend its fuel taxes amid the war in Iran, with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp approving a 60-day pause back in March.

  • Since then, at least five other states (including Ohio), have suspended, lowered or stopped increases in their fuel taxes. Kemp declared a state of emergency in late September and suspended the excise tax again for 30 days.
  • Utah cut its gas tax by some 15% through the end of the year. Gov. Andy Beshear (D-Ky.) froze an expected increase in the gas and diesel taxes in May. Illinois suspended its set increase this summer for six months.
  • Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) also suspended Indiana's gas tax in April. He renewed the suspension in late September and lifted restrictions on dyed diesel for farmers and timber harvesters.

Friction point: The Trump administration signaled openness to a gas tax holiday this spring, but Congress must suspend the levy. While the idea has been floated before, lawmakers have never done so.

  • Suspending the taxes can bring some relief to consumers, but it wouldn't offset the spikes they've felt at the pump since the start of the war. Plus, critics note doing so could increase the deficit and hurt the Highway Trust Fund it fuels.
  • But as Axios' Ben Geman noted back in May, political winds aren't always predictable — especially with drivers and truckers still feeling the strain months later, and as political messages cluster around cost-of-living concerns.

Zoom out: Other states have taken a similar approach to Braun by waiving seasonal and traditional restrictions for strained industries.

  • For example, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) directed state law enforcement to stop enforcing rules against dyed diesel, usually reserved for off-road machinery and exempt from taxes, "to relieve the state's agricultural and timber communities."
  • Louisiana, Nebraska, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Texas took similar action.
  • Still, other states pursued different avenues for relief: California recently took action to permit cheaper, winter-blend gas to be sold earlier than usual, while Michigan allowed gas stations to sell lower-cost gasoline earlier this spring.

The bottom line: Even if a federal gas tax holiday remains unlikely, pump pain — and perhaps, the possibility of future political pain — is fueling state action.

Go deeper: Iran war drives $100 billion in extra energy costs for U.S. consumers
